#6678. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Party Brought Everyone Out

There’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, with special thanks to the 1 Hotel West Hollywood.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

Midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. Garfield’s forthcoming Artificial (out December 25) is the movie on everybody’s lips, but he told me he’s looking forward to spending the holidays in New York and taking a brief break before what will probably be a busy campaign season for the Man of the Year.

No one captured the evening as succinctly as Robby Hoffman, who described her upcoming TV show as “Curb [Your Enthusiasm] for poor people.” When the conversation turned back to GQ, Hoffman rued the decline of magazine paper quality. But this latest issue got her seal of approval: appropriately glossy, well-considered, and elite to the touch. Though she might have just been describing the party’s guest list.

But even if you didn’t make the cut, you can see how GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party looked from the inside. ✦

#6677. Pamela Anderson Is a Sentimentalist at Heart

The actress on holiday traditions, motherhood, and the sentimental value of giving with Pandora.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

For Pamela Anderson, the holiday season is less about elaborate celebrations and more about appreciating life’s quieter moments. “I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul,” she tells ELLE. Whether she’s tending to her garden on Vancouver Island, cooking vegetarian dishes for her family, or watching her sons establish traditions of their own, Anderson has found a new appreciation for the simple pleasures that make this time of year so special.

It’s a philosophy that extends to her approach to gift-giving. A self-described sentimentalist, Anderson prefers presents that carry a personal meaning, from family photographs to jewelry passed down through generations. And through her partnership with Pandora (Anderson is a face of the brand), she’s found a way to celebrate those connections with pieces that feel both personal and accessible.

I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul. I think that’s a Virginia Woolf quote. Even in a garden, you focus more on the little things instead of being overwhelmed by so much abundance. It feels like a really special time of year. I love the fall weather and the leaves changing. It’s beautiful, especially here on the East Coast. Where I’m from on Vancouver Island, it actually looks very similar.

I absolutely love gardening. When I was home, I was cleaning up a bunch of leaves, and it feels like a workout, too. It’s nice to be outside, even in the rain. I don’t shy away from the rain, or nothing would ever get done where I’m from. I love being outside and getting my hands dirty. In this part of my life, I’m really gravitating toward that, but I’m also working a lot, so it’s a really good balance. I get to do really glamorous things, work on film and onstage, and then I go home, put my boots on, and get in the garden.

Now, the boys are usually with their wife and fiancée over the holidays. They’re building their lives and their own traditions, so I always say, “Don’t worry about me. I’m always around.” It’s nice to see them building those traditions. I’ve done a lot of hosting and party planning in my life. I’m a decorator, so I love all of that. But this year, it’s really about seeing all the traditions and things my sons have soaked up and watching them start their own lives. I’m not a pressure planner. I don’t want them to feel pressure to include me. I just say, “You guys do your thing. I’m watching, I’m observing.” It’s really special as a mom to see them so happy with their significant others. The women in their lives have great taste and love to share that with them and me.

I love cooking. I always cook all the sides, the vegetable dishes. It’s been a while since we’ve all been together for a big meal. Time is just flying by. My sons are such great cooks, too. We all have our specialties. I think I actually prefer decorating to cooking, because you set the stage. Then you can have a potluck!

I’ve given a lot of my jewelry from my lifetime to my kids and to their wife and fiancée. I like more sentimental gifts. I’m a sentimentalist, I guess. I love flowers, and this year, one of my sons just got married, but they don’t have wedding pictures of themselves. So they’re getting wedding pictures, engagement pictures, just a bunch of really sentimental things from me.

I just give my kids everything. I like to give those pieces to them so they can appreciate them while I’m here. I don’t hoard a lot of things. I’m always changing, always trying new things, and I don’t think I’m a big consumer anyway. I have special pieces that I’ve already passed on.

My mother always wants my Pandora jewelry. Every time I go anywhere, she’s asking, “Do you have Pandora? Do you have any earrings?” She loves it. My mom’s sisters and everyone just love Pandora. She loves both gold and silver, the jewels, the colors. Some of the beautiful pieces they have around the holidays, she would go crazy for. She loves it all.

I definitely wear more jewelry than I used to. It depends on what I’m wearing or where I’m going. I like to recycle jewelry. A lot of my Pandora pieces I’ve worn on different red carpets or to different special events. It’s nice for jewelry to be attainable, cruelty-free, and sustainable. Those things are so important to me. Jewelry isn’t just for the few. It’s for everybody.

When I align with somebody, I like to know that we have similar philosophies. I think it’s the small-town girl in me who never felt jewelry was in the cards for her. It’s nice to know there’s a jewelry company that’s forward-thinking and sustainable, thinking about recycling and also making it affordable. It just feels more like me. I love glamour and I love fancy things, but I think my kind of fashion is more inspirational.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6676. All the Photos of Princess Kate and Prince William on Their Overseas Tour of Mumbai

The royal pair will spend three days in India for the 2026 Earthshot Prize Awards

On Monday, November 16, Princess Kate and Prince William landed in Mumbai, India, for their first overseas royal tour in four years. The last time the pair made an international state visit was when they traveled to the Caribbean in the spring of 2022 to celebrate the late Queen Elizabeth II’s Platinum Jubilee.

Now, the Prince and Princess of Wales have hit the road again for the 2026 Earthshot Prize Awards, which are being hosted in Asia for the first time ever. The annual prize, founded by Prince William with an inaugural ceremony in 2021 and set to last until 2030, celebrates innovators who are breaking ground in the environmentalism space.

While it was announced back in February that William would be traveling for the ceremony, it was confirmed only this past weekend that Kate would be joining him. This marks her first major trip with William since her 2024 cancer diagnosis and eventual remission (she also took a solo trip to Italy this May).

The 2026 Earthshot ceremony takes place on November 17, but Kate and William are spending a total of three days in India. They began their trip with a visit to Ballard Estate, the business and shopping district of Mumbai. There, the Prince and Princess of Wales played a bit of gully cricket, took a ride on the metro, and visited local vendors and performers. Then, on day two, they stopped by the Bandra Worli Sea Link promenade and attended the Children’s Earthshot ceremony before dressing up for the official event.

For the rest of their time abroad, the royals will be “celebrating innovation, sustainability, youth leadership, and the enduring connections between the United Kingdom and India,” per their office at Kensington Palace.

#6674. Was This the Biggest Week in Sneakers of 2026?

As we inch towards the end of the year, there’s always a massive holiday rush in the sneaker industry (in addition to, well, everywhere else). Annual seasonal drops like the reliable Black Friday and Holiday XI launches from Jordan Brand, plus every major label trying to end the year on the highest note possible, make November and December some of the most exciting times to be a sneakerhead. To be fair, 2026 certainly still has some gas in the tank—plenty of us are already looking ahead to the return of the “Space Jam” Air Jordan 11 next month. Still, this week stands out even in an already crowded release calendar—in fact, I’m inclined to say it’s the biggest and best week of sneaker releases this year has had to offer so far.

Nike and Adidas lead the way with collaborations from massive designers and some up-and-comers alike, including one release that makes a strong argument for being the best sneaker of the year. Reebok’s gradual revitalization takes a massive step in a fun, innovative new direction. And over at Converse, one of the most reliable celebrity designers in the footwear world is dropping some of his best work yet. Start drafting an apology letter to your credit card for everything you’re about to do with it—these are just a few highlights from the biggest, boldest week of sneakers in 2026 yet.

Who said anything about Samba fatigue? Turns out all it takes to make one of the most gen-pop shoes of the last decade feel brand new is a take like the one offered this week by Adidas Consortium collaborator Invincible, a Taiwanese brand that’s quickly establishing itself as a can’t-miss partner for the Three Stripes. Alongside a stellar line of apparel the brand has savvily outmaneuvered any semblance of cultural exhaustion with one of Adidas’s signature silhouettes by keeping it simple: They’ve outfitted the silhouette in a premium black unstructured leather and, bafflingly, a dress shoe sole rather than the Samba’s traditional gum rubber. With perforated Stripes and detailing that mimics those found on dressy leather brogues, it’s an instant contender for sneaker of the year…even if it just barely qualifies as one. This one goes on sale on November13, but with a catch—it’s an Asia exclusive. Pray to the resale market gods.

Nike has been struggling to find their next big-name collaborator, but in the meantime, some old favorites are still holding strong. One of those names is Union, the Los Angeles-based boutique founded by streetwear giant Chris Gibbs. This week, the brand is offering a buzzy iteration on the classic Nike Dunk that comes in a luxe brown suede and a heel-less mule silhouette. Like the Invincible Samba, the MO here is that all it takes to make an old shoe feel new again is a left-of-center take. These are dropping via SNKRS and Union on November 13, for $130 a pop.

Through Reebok’s ups and downs over the last decade, there has been one shining constant: Allen Iverson, the greatest athlete they’ve ever had on their roster. AI’s shoes are always in style, so if the brand simply brought back the original Question Mid silhouette for the shoe’s 30th anniversary, it’d be noteworthy enough. This year, though, they’ve taken the shoe to a new and fairly innovative space, refitting it with modern performance enhancements, making it court-worthy for the first time in decades. Sure, you can still wear them with oversized tees and baggy shorts. But for the first time in ages, the Question could also make it back onto an NBA court (or at least the pavement at your local park). It’s priced at $170 and is available now via Reebok and select retailers.

Ever since he first inked a deal with Converse in 2017, Tyler, the Creator has been one of the best celebrity collaborators in the sneaker biz. This has only become more true since the launch of the 1908 Project last year. The endeavor has seen the pair diving deep into Converse’s archive to revive everything from classic nautical boating shoes, to a jogging silhouette that hadn’t seen the light of day in decades. Ahead of Tyler’s annual Camp Flog Gnaw festival last year, he and Converse launched their best work at the time: the Bronco Boot, a canvas and rubber-toed banger of a sneaker-boot. This year, they’re running it back on a low-top Bronco Boot silhouette—once again ahead of the festival, where we’ll likely see Tyler wearing them. Think of it as the Doc Martens 1461 to the original Bronco Boot’s Doc Martens 1460. Coming your way in four earthy colorways, these are on sale now via Converse.

Speaking of Converse and boots: One of the biggest sneaker stories of the year has been Rick Owens’s return to Adidas after a fruitful stint over at Converse. The designer’s much-anticipated return collection launched this week, with these stunners at the center of the capsule. Debuting on the runway at Paris Fashion Week this past summer, Owens’s Springblade boots are a showstopper of a return. The shoe’s upper is made from a loose textile that fits up over the ankle and a leather toe cap, but the real heat comes in the return of the Springblade sole Owens and Adidas first debuted over ten years ago. They retail for a crazy $850, and can be purchased via the Adidas Confirmed app. Rick’s gonna Rick!

#6673. Beyond the Blueprint: The Art of Building an Architectural Legacy

What does it take to create something that truly endures? How can luxury leaders balance heritage with innovation and create spaces that are not only beautiful but meaningful to the people who inhabit them? Against the backdrop of London’s iconic Tower Bridge, some of the leading names in luxury gathered aboard one of the world’s most extraordinary superyachts, Kismet, for an afternoon spent discussing the legacies they hope to leave behind.

These questions brought together influential leaders across fashion, jewelry, architecture, real estate, retail, and technology for an exclusive Vogue Business gathering in collaboration with Shanna Collective. Held on October 14, with London's historic skyline as its setting and the superyacht itself offering a compelling example of ambitious design, the event explored what it takes to create spaces, brands, and experiences that transcend generations. Hosted by Shanna Khan, founder and CEO of Shanna Collective, the afternoon opened with remarks from Vogue Business head of advisory and custom insights Anusha Couttigane, followed by a panel moderated by Vogue Business features director Lucy Maguire. Speakers included Sergei Mosunov, CEO of Fabergé; Jade Holland Cooper, founder and creative director of Holland Cooper; and Dr Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE, chief executive of the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA).

“Hosting this gathering with Vogue Business aboard Kismet was a wonderful opportunity to convene thought leaders from architecture, hospitality, real estate, and retail, each bringing a distinct perspective on the future of design and placemaking to build an enduring legacy,” said Khan. “What struck me was the shared understanding that creating something truly exceptional requires more than a vision for the space itself; it requires an understanding of its wider context, its people, and the legacy it can leave behind. Anusha and I were delighted to bring this group together, and I left feeling inspired by the ambition, openness, and collective thinking in the room,” she added.

Left to right: Lucy Maguire (features director, Vogue Business), Jade Holland Cooper (founder and CEO, Holland Cooper), Anusha Couttigane (head of advisory and custom insights, Vogue Business), Shanna Khan (founder and CEO, Shanna Collective) and Dr. Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE (CEO, RIBA).

Opening the discussion, Couttigane drew parallels between London’s architectural history and the role of private enterprise in shaping cities.

“If you look out across the city, you can observe centuries of architectural ambition, entrepreneurship, and reinvention.” she began. “It’s a reminder that the great cities we inherit today weren’t shaped by architects and politicians alone. They were also shaped by entrepreneurs, investors, and business leaders who saw opportunities to create something bigger than themselves — investing in the physical landscape, advancing commerce and culture, and creating places that would serve communities for generations,” she continued.

The English capital also holds a symbolic place in Khan’s business philosophy. “It was no coincidence that we gathered in the heart of London, a city that shaped that modern world and one that hosted us for discussions on how we can collectively steward the future,” Khan said. Having recently been interviewed by Couttigane for Vogue Business, Khan’s own work includes the regeneration of Chicago’s Fulton Market district and Jacksonville’s Shipyards development, where design, commerce, and community intersect.

“What I find particularly compelling about Shanna’s approach is her conviction that exceptional design should do more than create beautiful buildings and interiors. It should contribute something enduring to the places and people around it. It should honor the past and the history of a place, while making it relevant for modern users. It’s a philosophy that resonates strongly with our discussion today,” Couttigane added.

Anusha Couttigane delivering the opening remarks.

Beginning the panel, Maguire asked Mosunov how Fabergé is translating the hallmarks of the brand, such as craftsmanship, detail, and surprise into the physical realm, given its ambitions to expand physically. “The previous owner had a business model that was focused on B2B. It didn’t have its own retail distribution. When I bought Fabergé, I decided that we needed to expand the direct-to-consumer business, with the main instrument being our own boutiques,” Mosunov explained.

The challenge is creating spaces that communicate the maison’s heritage while supporting its contemporary ambitions. “We needed to express this historical story through the boutiques, showcasing pre-1970 pieces and sharing the story about Peter Carl Fabergé, the founder of the company. This way, you get a real sense of the company.” Mosunov also shared how the brand is designing jewelry iterations of its iconic egg motifs, inspired by the fifty Imperial Eggs that secured the maison’s acclaim between 1885 and 1916.

As Fabergé expands its international retail footprint, Mosunov is adapting the design of its boutiques to local preferences. “For example, in the Middle East, we have a store in the Dubai Mall. They like very opulent forms in that region so we need to adapt the execution to the local marketplace.”

Vaughan-Dick reinforced the importance of cultural context in architecture. Referencing Norman Foster’s work in the Middle East, she highlighted the influence of climate, environment and local requirements on architectural decisions. “You cannot have this homogenous view of design. You have to think about culture, sustainability, and building safety. You have to look at the different requirements for that country and for that particular society,” she added.

Turning to Holland Cooper, Maguire asked about how she was creating environments that would resonate with the world of the brand. As a business that has grown from stalls at Badminton Horse Trials to a £100m+ company with flagship boutiques and a new 70,000-square-foot HQ in the Cotswolds, Holland Cooper spoke about the importance of making the brand experience as special as possible.

Left to right: Lucy Maguire (features director, Vogue Business), Dr. Valerie Vaughan-Dick MBE (CEO, RIBA), Sergei Mosunov (owner and CEO, Fabergé) and Jade Holland Cooper (founder and CEO, Holland Cooper).

“Although we don’t have a lot of shops, the ones that we do have are so important.” she explained. “For me, the importance of retail is making that physical experience as special as we possibly can. I think there’s a narrative that retail is dead, that bricks and mortar is dead, but I think we’re just getting too lazy about the experience that we’re creating for the customer…what we’ve done in our physical retail spaces is really understand that the service and environment are paramount to that experience,” she added.

Holland Cooper’s retail philosophy draws inspiration from brands including Ralph Lauren and Abercrombie & Fitch, whose distinctive environments left a lasting impression on her as a young shopper: “I am pedantic about music volume, lighting, smell, hanger presentation, visual merchandising, how the staff and the service levels are, because the minute you walk through those doors, you want it to be immersive, and you want people to forget the outside world. That’s why they call it retail therapy.”

Maguire then highlighted a tension in the theme: “Buildings need to endure, but the people, communities, and lifestyles they serve are constantly changing. How should brands, architects and developers design for longevity without becoming trapped by the tastes or assumptions of the present?” she asked.

For Vaughan-Dick, the guiding architectural principle is “long life, loose fit”: creating buildings capable of adapting to future needs. “I do think that individuals recognize that when you’re designing buildings, they don’t know what a building is going to look like in 100 years time, but every architect, every engineer, everyone here needs to think: what we design now needs to have that longer life,” she stated.

Left to right: Tom Pascall (communications manager, the Chancery Rosewood), Joanna Gunn (chief brand officer, Rosewood), Shanna Khan (CEO and founder, Shanna Collective) and Naomi Sebley (the Chancery Rosewood).

For Mosunov, Fabergé’s design legacy distinguishes between timeless beauty, modern beauty, and more transient aesthetic preferences when considering its future. Holland Cooper similarly sees heritage as an enduring source of differentiation: “I am obsessive about heritage, classic shapes and just reinventing them to be appealing to the modern audience, and that doesn’t mean ripping the rulebook up entirely. I pay homage to all the beautiful British aesthetics, and that’s the romanticism of what we’re doing, really,” said Holland Cooper.

As a consequence, British manufacturing remains fundamental to the brand’s identity and ambitions. “All of our tailoring is made in London. All of the wool is woven in the UK, and I’ve done that since day one. And I was told that it wouldn’t be possible to scale a business and do that, and I have, and it is. And I’m really passionate about the UK manufacturing industry. So that’s a big part of our heritage,” she explained.

For Khan, these principles of detail, experience and emotional connection are paramount: “Jade shared her belief that every detail matters to drive an exuberant retail experience. Elements that may seem subtle influence how a place is experienced, remembered, and valued. For me, that is where design becomes truly meaningful: when we can transport guests in time and place, it moves beyond aesthetics to create an emotional connection that endures long after the initial experience itself.”

Left to right: Andrea Latten, (chief business officer, Condé Nast Britain), Shanna Khan (CEO and founder, Shanna Collective) and Christopher Warren (UK head of industry, Condé Nast Britain).

The afternoon concluded with a tour of Kismet, whose interior design was led by Shanna as chief creative director. The superyacht is an example of the extraordinary experiences that thoughtful design can create. For an industry deeply rooted in heritage, the gathering raised a pertinent question: what are today’s luxury leaders creating that will remain relevant and meaningful to future generations?

For Shanna Khan, working together across disciplines is central to answering this question. “Our collaboration with Vogue Business creates a valuable opportunity to bring different disciplines into our conversations and explore how ideas from across creative landscapes can inform one another. The future of luxury lies in creating places and experiences with substance, soul, and generational value,” she said. But she reflected: “Ultimately, building in an enduring way is defined by creating something that feels relevant today, salutes the heritage of the past, and has the potential to become part of a legacy for generations to come.”

#6672. Prince William and Kate Wear Traditional Indian Designs to Attend the Earthshot Prize Awards in Mumbai

The princess accessorized her intricate gown with Queen Elizabeth’s fantastic emerald tassel suite

The Prince and Princess of Wales paid homage to Indian culture as they attended the sixth annual Earthshot Prize Awards tonight in Mumbai.

After a busy day of engagements (and outfit changes), the couple made it to the Jio World Convention Centre to celebrate global change-makers who are actively working to solve urgent environmental problems. It was the first time the awards were held in India, and the event brought together around 5,000 global guests, world leaders, and celebrities.

And for the momentous evening, the British royals wore traditional Indian attire.

Prince William went for a rare all-black look, the highlight of which was a traditional velvet Bandhgala jacket by Indian designer Manish Malhotra. By his side, Princess Catherine—at her first Earthshot ceremony since 2022—was a vision in a vermilion-red anarkali gown custom-made for her by Indian designer Mahima.

The stunning long-sleeve piece had gold and green embroidery throughout, and Kate expertly accessorized it with jewelry from Queen Elizabeth II’s fabulous emerald tassel suite. Up top, she wore the late monarch’s luxurious diamond-and-emerald tassel drop earrings, while around her neck, the matching tassel necklace took the spotlight.

The suite is believed to have been gifted to Queen Elizabeth by Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi during the 1989 United Arab Emirates state visit to Britain. And through the years, the monarch took it out for several important occasions, including for the Return Dinner hosted in 2011 by President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama at the end of their state visit to the United Kingdom.

In 2022, the queen loaned the suite to Kate, who wore the necklace and earrings to the state dinner hosted by the Governor General of Jamaica. Now, it’s become a shining standout in her royal jewelry collection.

#6668. Office Hours: Saie’s Laney Crowell on the Beauty of Doing Good

For Laney Crowell, “feel good, do good” is not just the core philosophy of her beauty brand, Saie, but how she lives her life. “So much of beauty is not only who you are on the inside, but the actions that you take,” she says, emphasizing “the importance of taking action, especially in things that you are excited and passionate about.”

The driving force behind Saie was Crowell’s growing desire to make beauty better by creating formulas that are not just safe for your skin but also good for it. She wanted to create products that spoke to her as a self-professed “expert consumer.” “I’ve always struggled with really sensitive, acne-prone skin,” she says. “I had an aha moment where I realized that my makeup was what was making me break out. I started a blog [called The Moment] to have the conversation. It was niche, but at the same time, I was one of the only people having this conversation.” Saie was born from this community building seven years ago.

The brand has steadily expanded since then, without ever straying from its mission. Each new product follows the same principles: It’s formulated to nourish the skin, is noncomedogenic, and is clinically tested and dermatologist tested. “When you try Saie, you immediately feel the textures and how hydrating they are. Then as you continue to use them, you realize how happy your skin is. You’re really seeing benefits over time.”

Saie’s innovations, however, haven’t come without growing pains. Working with a long list of ingredients to avoid, including silicones, the team has found that developing long-lasting products takes a long time. “I only ever want to launch something if it’s perfect,” Crowell says. Take its City Set setting spray, for example. When it debuted in December 2025, no setting spray claimed 16-hour wear.

“I make beauty products for women who get ready in five minutes, just like me,” says Crowell, who is gearing up to solve another customer request. Saie’s next launch, CityStick, took two years to perfect and is set to debut later this year. “I’m always on the go, so I wanted something I could throw in my bag, swipe on for a bit of radiance, and know I was also doing something good for my skin. That’s CityStick—my makeup and skin care in one quick step.” It’s 50% makeup, 50% skin care; expect the sheer, soft-focus, radiant coverage of a skin tint with the benefits of nourishing skin care.

Helming a cosmetics brand—not to mention pioneering an entire category—requires vision and tenacity, two things Crowell has in equal measure. The last seven years have shown her just how resilient she is. “The most important attribute of a founder and entrepreneur is the ability to keep going,” she says. The other thing she’s learned? How much she loves to improve. “I am always thinking about how I, the brand, and everything that we do get 1% better every day.”

Beyond formulating, leading, and championing a host of climate initiatives (the brand has Planet Beautiful, an annual sustainability and plastic-recovery campaign in partnership with Sephora and RePurpose Global), Crowell is also a mother of two. She’s as passionate about Saie’s commitment to our planet (read: making systemic change regarding the billions of units of plastic the beauty industry generates each year) as she is about showing up for her two little girls.

“My weekdays are crazy, but I love it,” she says with a laugh. Days at her home upstate start with a 6:30 a.m. matcha (Rocky’s ceremonial-grade matcha with steamed oat milk and simple syrup she makes herself) and a workout (weight training or Pilates) before the kids wake up. After getting them ready and taking them to school (her favorite part of the day), she’ll make another matcha, then settle in for a marathon of Zoom calls before spending the evening with the kids. She comes into the city once a week to meet with her team in person; The Mercer is her home away from home.

As an entrepreneur, she’s keen to take care of herself by consciously putting herself first, including upholding her boundaries. “When you do something that you really love, I think that is also a really beautiful commitment to yourself,” she says.

Having started her business at the tail end of 2019, Crowell worked tirelessly during the pandemic, when she also gave birth to her second child, Rosie. “I think back on the success of Saie, and a big part of it is that for two years I basically worked the amount that most people do in, like, six years,” she says. Her days were a balance of work and breastfeeding, and she only really left the house to go for walks. “After that, my immune system was a mess,” she adds. Working with holistic coach Jill Ketner Villa was her saving grace. Years later, Crowell says Villa is her “secret weapon” as a founder. Through her work with the practitioner, she’s developed her supplement ritual; she takes approximately 15 a day. Her assortment includes magnesium, zinc, iron, and vitamins C, A, and D—all housed in a beautiful leather pill case.

She’s also been meditating for 12 years. Nowadays, she loves Gabrielle Bernstein’s guided meditations, which last 10 to 20 minutes. “I get a lot of clarity out of it, and I find it to be the best way to calm anxiety.” Sleep, of course, is another tranquil practice; practice is the operative word because Crowell does a lot to ensure she gets a good night’s sleep. She takes magnesium or CBD before bed and uses the Truvaga device to stimulate her vagus nerve system and regulate her circadian rhythm. “Then I have my humidifier, face mask, earplugs, always a thick lip balm—that usually does it.” (The humidifier also makes its way to her weekly stays at The Mercer.)

Otherwise, she says going on a walk in nature helps her be her best self. “If I can fit a walk in between Zooms, that is a good day. I have my best ideas on walks.”

Crowell’s skin philosophy is appropriately minimalist, largely to suit her sensitive, dry, acne-prone skin. “I don’t use a ton of products, and I don’t use anything that’s super active. Generally, ‘less is more’ is what’s right for my skin, with a heavy focus on hydration.” As someone so knowledgeable and passionate about formulation, she’s gotten her skin-care regimen down to a science and has a couple of brands she knows work well for her skin.

First is Medik8, which she turns to for a suite of products: cleansers, a hydrating serum, and its Crystal Retinal. “Their retinol is the only retinol I can use. I use either level one, two, or three. I don’t really go above that. I also really love Sofie Pavitt’s line—it’s really wonderful if you have acne-prone skin.” Specifically, she gravitates toward the Omega Rich Moisturizer, Clean Clean Cleanser, and Mandelic Clearing Serum to spot-treat breakouts. Otherwise, she loves the Dr. Barbara Sturm toner for extra hydration, Alloy’s estrogen-powered face cream to boost skin’s plumpness, and Colorescience’s tinted mineral sunscreen if she’s skiing or in the sun, though her daily SPF is Saie’s Slip Tint. For extra protection, you’ll likely find her in a hat.

Crowell likes to keep her makeup routine quick. “I am not a makeup artist,” she says. “So all of our formulas are easy and effortless. I really love looking like myself.” Her five-minute regimen always starts with Saie’s Glowy Super Gel, which “gives [her] the most beautiful lit-from-within glow,” followed by Slip Tint for moisturizing coverage with sun protection. After a bit of Slip Tint concealer and a thoughtful dusting of the collection’s setting powder, she moves on to blush. At night she might layer the liquid Dew Blush and the powder SuperSuede blush, but for daytime it’s one or the other paired with the SuperSuede Baked Bronzer. Next, she brushes up her brows with gels by Kristie Streicher or Rare Beauty. Then she adds a mist of City Set setting spray, a few coats of Mascara 101, and her go-to lip combo (lip liner in shade Flirt, plus Glossybounce lip oil in shade Dip) for the finishing touches.

Hydration is key to keeping her thick, long brown hair, which can sometimes be dry, looking its best. “I don’t get a lot of haircuts, so I’m always hydrating the roots,” she says. Roz’s Milk Hair Serum comes with her everywhere, as does the brand’s Santa Lucia Styling Oil. “I really love her formulas,” she says. K18’s post-shower leave-in delivers molecular repair, while Arrey’s Not Today, Grey supplement slows early graying and supports fullness. “It’s 100% made a difference. When I stopped taking them, I noticed it.”

Another product she doesn’t leave home without is Dae’s styling wand, which comes in handy for taming flyaways. For her beloved beach waves, she swears by T3’s curling iron (specifically the 1-inch and 1.5-inch barrel sizes) and a bit of Dae’s styling cream.

Crowell is as thoughtful with her style as she is with her skin care and makeup. “I definitely believe in quality over quantity, so I wouldn’t say I buy a lot,” she says. When she does shop, however, she always asks herself if the item fits her “’90s, a little sporty, and minimalist” ethos. That said, she gravitates toward pieces from The Row, Khaite, and Kallmeyer or really special vintage finds. Most days, you’ll find her in jeans, a T-shirt, and Adidas sneakers—or Manolos to dress things up.

#6666. Jennifer Lopez Pours Us a Straight Dose of Holiday Cheer With Her Parade of Festive Fashion

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Jennifer Lopez will never enter a room quietly. The “Proof of Love” singer is one for maximalist luxury—with her collection of Hermès bags, sky-high stilettos, shimmery catsuits, and fur coats—and now that the air has turned crisp, she’s doing holiday dressing the J.Lo way.

This week, the superstar has been in New York City promoting her concert special “The JLo Show: Live in Las Vegas” which premieres on November 26, as well as her new holiday collection of JLo Beauty Beso Balms. And if anyone knows how to dress for a promotional tour, it’s Lopez.

On Sunday, she kicked things off strong with a head-to-toe crimson look. A sheer candy apple-red pussy-bow blouse was tucked into silky matching shorts and layered under a cherry leather trench. For even more drama, Lopez slipped into a pair of red flower-print tights and rouge snakeskin pumps with golden stilettos. A Tom Ford alligator clutch in a deep apple red added the final monochrome touch, while diamond jewelry brought the shimmer to the Christmas-core ensemble.

Also on Sunday, Lopez changed into a sandy suede Retrofête minidress and chocolate pumps for an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. And she did several festive quick changes while on stage for the “Wig Swap Holiday Lounge Singers” bit.

Today, to attend Sirius XM’s Front Row, J.Lo wore a very different, but equally holiday-appropriate look. Leaning intro the traditional colors of the Christmas season—red and green—Lopez wore a sheer green top tucked into sheer burgundy tights and layered it all with mixed-metal chain belts.

An embellished cinnamon-brown jacket pulled the look together. And for a dose of jewel tones, Lopez popped on a pair of suede grape-colored heels (which matched her underwear) and carried a satin turquoise bag.

A shaggy black faux-fur coat from Auter kept her warm as she stepped outside the studio.

Most recently, on Instagram, the Office Romance star debuted what is maybe her most festive look of the week. A fluffy white fur coat from Valentino that was belted at the waist with a black leather bow and paired with black accessories: tights, pointy heels, a clutch, and oversize sunglasses. Oh, and don’t forget the extravagant diamond jewelry from the Back Vault x David Webb.

It seems it’s time to get out that holiday wardrobe, and we all better step it up.

#6665. The Greatest Grand Theft Auto Missions, Definitively Ranked

Grand Theft Auto VI drops on November 19th, and there are many ways to prepare. I’ve been replaying every game going back to the original, with a particular soft spot for the 3D era: III, Vice City, and Rockstar's greatest achievement, San Andreas—yes, yes, I'm coming in hot. After some 13 years of GTA Online, with its perpetual content stream and microtransactions, it’s easy to forget how it all began. The franchise has consistently brought freewheeling chaos and mayhem, sure. But it has also always delivered memorable story missions, which evolved from basic lures and assassinations into something like GTA V's “Friend Request or “Reuniting the Family,” culturally scathing mini-movies which have to be played to be believed. “My least favorite mission involves Michael using a tattoo gun on me,” former Rockstar director, writer, and producer Lazlow Jones told me of the latter mission. “I still give Dan [Houser] shit about that one to this day.”

What follows is a ranking of the greatest missions in the series’ history, with one caveat: I only allowed myself four missions per game, maximum. To help sort through the clear classics and happy accidents, I talked to some of the people who made these games come alive, including Jones, former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, and West Coast rapper Young Maylay, the beloved voice of Carl Johnson. Shockingly, Maylay says he’s still fond of the infamous “Wrong Side of the Tracks.” “All we had to do was follow the damn train, CJ!” Maylay said, imitating his exasperated sensei Big Smoke. I’m not including that mission on here, though, partly because I’d like to make it out of this piece alive.

Bum. Budupup-budum. For a lot of us, that theme was the beginning of our Grand Theft Auto journey. What follows is barely prologue. There's an ambush on the Callahan Bridge, an escape with 8-Ball, and a drive to a safe house in Portland, Liberty City's Brooklyn-by-way-of-Queens industrial borough. You do not fire a single shot. And yet each playthrough already looked different. Did you open the short manual and splay the map across your bedroom floor, or drive blind to the edge of the Red Light District?

"The most memorable mission for me was the first one I ever played, 'Give Me Liberty,'" Lazlow told GQ. Once the host of Technofile, a syndicated show about technology and video games, Lazlow showed up at Rockstar’s Manhattan offices in 2001 to report a radio piece. Not long after, he was spoofing American radio himself as the iconic voice of Chatterbox FM.

"[Rockstar co-founder] Terry Donovan brought over a copy of the game the day it came out. Dan [Houser] had given me a PlayStation 2,” Lazlow continued. “I'd worked on the radio for the game all summer with Dan but I hadn't actually seen it. After the cinematic ended, I got into the car and Head Radio came on and I'm driving through town. It blew my mind."

Crazy what a difference three years can make. The Donald Love of GTA III is a composed real-estate scion with a media empire. Liberty City Stories, set in 1998, shows you the man before the polish, who’s way more overt about his hunger for power — and human flesh.

The mayoral race is his project, and Toni Cipriani is his instrument. Toni guns down the incumbent mayor R.C. Hole, somehow engendering only one star. "Steering the Vote" then puts him behind the wheel of a campaign van, zooming across Staunton while the loudspeaker blares: “O'Donovan is a communist!” “O’Donovan hates America!” or “A vote for Love is a vote for happiness!” The van has to reach specific stops before the messaging triggers, which means the game is literally grading you on how much of the world you can seduce. GTA may have predicted everything from Ozempic culture to billionaire doomsday prep, but there was no forecast sharper than this one.

For most of Rockstar’s history, the studio—technically a U.S. company, but with a British development team—has made its bread and butter satirizing America, and nothing has been off the table. But in London 1969, the first of two expansion packs for the original Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar transplants its crime sandbox to London in the late ‘60s, where the Brits take center stage. (“Who gave Paul McCartney a shotgun?” one YouTube commenter asks.) Broken up into chapters, the seminal “Dead Certainty” draws on the high-flying exploits of the real-life Kray twins, the foremost perpetrators of organized crime in London’s East End at the time, who rubbed elbows with politicians and entertainers before ultimately being locked away for life.

Grand Theft Auto is a game about many things, but one of the first things it was—and still is—is a game about cars. If San Fierro’s underrated main story missions aren’t enough (yes, I know, Cesar. The yay is leaving San Fierro again), head on over to Easter Basin for the best edition of “Exports and Imports.” The concept dates back to the original GTA, where it was called “Crane Bonuses,” but it’s a classic here because of its sheer scale. What starts at the docks turns into a mad hunt across the entire map of San Andreas, finding and then delivering 30 specific vehicles.

San Andreas has 212 defined vehicles, more than twice as many as Vice City. You start learning the taxonomy—how to tell a Remington from a Sabre and an Infernus from a Cheetah—and figuring out where certain vehicles turn up. The Camper can be found on top of Mount Chiliad, meaning the hard part isn’t finding it so much as getting the lumbering thing back down in one piece. When I was younger, I never really appreciated these side missions. Now, I love how they slow the game down and make you observe all the GTA sandbox goodness you might otherwise race past.

Rockstar has a long, cruel history of giving you a remote control and trolling. But unlike “Supply Lines” or “Demolition Man,” there’s a certain genius to this one. Vic Vance pulls up outside the Mendez compound and, instead of going in like a cowboy, climbs into a van to command a newfangled robot servant, Domestobot. At this point the game becomes a butlering simulator: Fetch a drink, light a cigar, and clean the floor, all the while trying to crack a drug kingpin’s basement safe. Rockstar didn’t forget about our charming robot after this, either. In GTA V, Radio Los Santos host Big Boy laments the Domestobot future that never arrived: "We have internet glasses, but not our own robot butler!”

In 1995, at age 17, Blair Renaud joined what became Rockstar Canada (now Rockstar Toronto), and stuck around long past his original contract, eventually becoming a technical director. “I basically walked into the boss's office and was like, ‘I'm not leaving. I'll do whatever you want,'” Renaud told me. After designing the London ‘69 map without ever having set foot in England (“I just winged it”), he and his entire Toronto office were put on QA duty for Grand Theft Auto 2, with its grim retro-futurist Anywhere City and sharper graphics.

GTA has always played with consumption (Donald Love likely ate his real estate mentor, Avery Carrington) but “Hot Dog Homicide!” is GTA2 at its most dastardly. In the original PC/Dreamcast version, you steal a bus, load it with civilian passengers, and deliver them to a Russian mob boss's meat grinder to satiate his army. “I think [GTA] was actually more controversial [in the beginning] about the crime, rather than just the violence,” Renaud said. “It was like ‘Oh, I'm like stealing people's cars and running them over.' It was a little bit more real.” For all the creative choices the series has been pilloried for in the ensuing years, a mission like “Hot Dog Homicide!” wasn't nearly as explosive then as it would be today.

I always get excited about missions that let you revisit a location you've already seen, especially when the game gives you a reason to see it differently. “Bury the Hatchet” sends Michael and Trevor back to North Yankton, the snowy Midwestern state where GTA V began, where the two men start digging into the events of the botched bank heist that set their lives on their current course.

It’s San Andreas’s “St. Mark’s Bistro” done better. Instead of briefly dropping you into a familiar location for a quick hit of nostalgia, GTA V actually lets you spend some time knee-deep in the snow. Michael and Trevor each retrace the events of the heist; Trevor unearths a coffin marked with Michael’s name, only to find Brad’s decomposing body inside. Ultimately, the two men aim guns at each other. Michael has spent much of the game on his high horse insisting that he’s changed, while Trevor, always the firecracker, is at least honest about exactly who he is.

Another great LCS mission that adds to Liberty City lore. Donald Love sends Toni to explosives expert 8-Ball (who still has functioning hands at this point) to raze an entire neighborhood, Fort Staunton, and pave the way for his Panlantic deal. With the Forellis giving chase, Toni has to get a van loaded with explosives to the site, then race through tunnels planting charges beneath the neighborhood. No way those tunnels aren’t at least a little inspired by Die Hard with a Vengeance. After the biggest explosion in GTA history (not bad for a PSP game), the National Guard can be found roaming the neighborhood. And by GTA III, Fort Staunton is teeming with scaffolding, construction pits and Cartel members, a neighborhood still reshaping itself after Toni’s seismic contribution.

There are few things more San Andreas than being handed a shoddy military plane by a mysterious government agent and being told to fly it across the state without being detected by radar. “N.O.E.” is the greatest test of your skills acquired in the Pilotwings-esque gauntlet, “Learning to Fly.” Fly too high and the military shoots you down; fly too low and the terrain dings you first. The mission captures just how far Mike Toreno has pulled CJ from the streets and into the shadowy world of government conspiracies.

Greg Johnson, a hip-hop journalist who became Rockstar's senior researcher from 2003 to 2020, traces those wild Toreno missions to the 1992 film Deep Cover. Most people know it through its title song, Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg's first record together. But the film itself touched on government corruption and drug trafficking in Southern California.

“Loved that Dan [Houser] put some Deep Cover-inspired missions in GTA SA with Mike Toreno basically playing Agent Carver and CJ as John Hull,” Johnson said. “I definitely talked to [Houser] a lot about Deep Cover, but he was also having conversations with [West Coast hip-hop producer and Rockstar writer] DJ Pooh, who personally knows [drug lord] Freeway Rick [Ross] about that era, and reading up on books and reports…as they wrote the game.”

Heavy metal band Love Fist is in a pickle. Think Speed, only with a limo, and even thicker Scottish accents than Groundskeeper Willie. The mission is straightforward, but not easy: drive the limousine across the city while keeping the momentum steady enough to hold off detonation. It’s also a testament to how Vice City could turn even its tertiary characters into stars. Love Fist barely occupies a sliver of the game, yet they've stuck around as memorable rockstars for more than two decades. Obbe Vermeij, longtime Rockstar North technical director, also has a soft spot for the mission. “Particularly funny,” he notes, “because the Love Fist voices are just guys from the office.”

There isn't a single on-rails shooting sequence in Grand Theft Auto that I've ever passed easily. Doesn't matter how many times I've played. I’m no deadeye. Luckily, in “Reuniting the Families,” there’s plenty packed in before we get to that. This is back when CJ, Sweet, Ryder and Big Smoke are all still homies, and when the vast map of San Andreas is still centered on the few-mile radius around Grove Street. You head to a motel with the intention of saving the hood, only to find it crawling with SWAT. After battling your way through the rooms and taking down a helicopter on the roof, you escape by car with the cops still in pursuit. Smoke is behind the wheel while an AK with unlimited ammo is placed in your hands. The cops can even climb onto the car and try to wrestle the gun away from you. It’s a wild, arcade-style sequence, but also one of the last hurrahs for the homies before betrayal and more nonsense from that bastard Frank Tenpenny. Fittingly, the getaway car flies straight through a Sprunk soda billboard reading “A Taste of Things to Come.”

“Cop Land” is peak bromance between Tommy and Lance, before the latter decides to ruin the movie. It’s also a snapshot of just how much more active and assertive Vice City’s main character is than man-of-no-words Claude, made all the more credible by the late Ray Liotta’s swagger in the role. Tommy isn't merely taking orders and working his way up someone else's criminal ladder. By this point, he's building the Vercetti Estate into his own empire and making his own destiny.

In “Cop Land,” the entire northern portion of the first island experiences a demographic shake up and now consists of exactly two assets: cops on foot in tan and brown and cops in green police cruisers. First, Tommy and Lance have to steal cop uniforms, a step that can get clunkier than it should when the garage door won't shut with the right number of cops inside. From there, you head to North Point Mall in disguise, plant a bomb and hightail it out of there with a five-star wanted level. Vice City’s officers were particularly bloodthirsty, and getting to a Pay 'n' Spray with Lance still intact—my man is drawn to dumb deaths—was one of my greatest teenage achievements.

Dubai-born real estate heir Yusuf Amir can buy anything. So naturally, the thing he wants most is an experimental attack helicopter parked on an arms dealer’s yacht. Rockstar was mining Gulf excess for laughs more than a decade before Dubai Bling and Love Is Blind: Habibi. Yusuf’s gaudy apartment tells you everything you need to know about him. There’s a miniature model of Algonquin laid out in his penthouse, as if the entire city were already one of his properties, and a giant dollar sign mounted on the wall. He dances to “Arab Money,” peppers his speech with hip-hop slang, and adopts the mannerisms of a culture he knows nothing about. Luis, unsurprisingly, is not particularly moved.

That makes “Sexy Time” the perfect introduction to him. Boat out from the marina, slip past the patrol and steal the Buzzard. Only, mid-flight, Yusuf calls and asks you to turn around, blow the yacht apart and run down what’s left of the arms dealers. For those who felt GTA IV took itself way too seriously, The Ballad of Gay Tony was a breath of fresh air. “Yusuf Amir is one of my all time favorite characters Dan [Houser] created,” Lazlow said. “The dialogue in this mission is hysterical, and he's constantly trying to sound street while going on about building luxury condos.”

The final chapter in the InterGlobal Studios asset arc turns Vice City into a formidable platformer. Tune in to Flash FM (Talk Talk’s “Life’s What You Make It”) or Fever 105 (Kool & The Gang’s “Summer Madness”) as Tommy leaps across rooftops on his trusted PCJ-600 bike in a single bound—though it’s far more likely that you’ll tumble to the streets at least once. There’s a delicate balance required for each stunt jump, but also a sense of reward once you master timing and speed.

This mission is, as the kids say, vibes. Something about scaling the ‘80s skyline by night while the rest of the city sleeps is unforgettable, along with the hilarious payoff, when Tommy triggers a spotlight that projects a massive X-rated image promoting adult performer Candy Suxxx (née Candice Shand) onto the side of a building. The most memorable GTA characters have a way of appearing in multiple forms: voices on the radio, bodies in cutscenes and, here, as advertising beamed across the world itself.

Small-town America gets the GTA treatment in “The Paleto Score.” Michael, Franklin and Trevor roll into sleepy Paleto Bay to rob the Blaine County Savings Bank, but the getaway quickly becomes less Ocean’s Eleven and more like Terminator or even MechCommander. Even before the heist, Lester, the master of elaborate setups, proves to be an unlikely master of conflict resolution too. His dry little “Hello, Franklin” to break up another Michael and Trevor spat still has me in stitches.

What starts as a relatively conventional bank job becomes a slow, lumbering march through an entire town, with our antiheroes mowing down cops, SWAT and eventually the military along the way. There’s even a reward for going overboard. One of the gold-medal requirements is to fire more than 4,000 bullets — because apparently, just robbing a bank wasn’t impressive enough.

Every time we see our hippie friend The Truth, his missions get better. In the apex of his mission tree, “Black Project,” CJ infiltrates Area 69, Rockstar’s twist on Area 51. There’s a stealth way of entering the maximum security facility, but that’s not nearly as fun as going in guns blazing. The level abounds with hilarious one-liners (“Get the General Mills on the line!”) and lab announcements (“Tonight’s menu is posted in the canteen. Barf bags can be ordered from Human Resources.”).

After GTA III’s and Vice City’s limited interiors, San Andreas gives you lively environments like Area 69, where you can disappear down corridors, into laboratories and through underground tunnels. And once CJ steals the coveted jet pack prototype, it becomes a way to fast travel across the state of San Andreas, bringing a whole new perspective to the final hours of the game. “The Truth. He stayed high as a motherfucker talking about conspiracy theory shit,” Young Maylay said. “But he would hit it on the head.”

Niko spends much of GTA IV doing other people’s dirty work. By “Late Checkout,” the diamond deal has gone so badly that Ray Boccino has lost his money, his diamonds and what remained of his patience. Isaac Roth, the diamond dealer who helped blow up the deal, is hiding in the Majestic Hotel. Ray wants him dead.

This mission is a choose-your-own-adventure affair. You can take the elevator and fight your way up through the guards, floor by floor, or use the window-cleaning platform outside to reach the penthouse from above and then fight your way back down. Either way, Niko eventually has to work his way through the hotel, killing Roth and his associates before making his escape.

It’s Rockstar’s take on the Plaza Hotel, minus Tim Curry, turned into a bonafide shooting gallery. Bonus points if you shove the front desk manager, who may respond by hopping over the desk to fight his own bellman.

Phil? Phil Collins? That's right. The former Genesis drummer and self-styled “Little Elvis” made gaming history by becoming the first real-life celebrity to lend his name and likeness as well as his voice to GTA. Like Vice City, VCS is inspired by the ‘80s TV drama Miami Vice; Philip Michael Thomas, who played Ricardo Tubbs on the show, voices Lance Vance in both VC and VCS, and Collins, as it happens, guest-starred on the series in 1985, as con man Phil Mayhew.

In this mission the Mob is after the Brit, and Vic has to ward them off. It all comes to a head during “In the Air Tonight” at Hyman Memorial Stadium. You're up top clearing Forelli saboteurs looming in the rafters while Phil is down below working the crowd.

For the man voicing Vic, this history wasn't lost on anyone. "Miami Vice was literally my favorite show as a little boy," said voice actor Dorian Missick. "I still have pictures of me in what I call my Miami Vice suit. One year, my mom let me get a little suit that they used to wear, but the collar’s turned up. I wore something like that for Easter. So to me, it was my opportunity to kind of be on the Miami Vice episode that I never got a chance to do. So all of these things, the Phil Collins of it all, and just that energy of it — it was exciting to be a part of that."

“Caida Libre,” Spanish for “free fall,” is one of those missions that finally makes the sprawling expanse of GTA V’s San Andreas feel like one cohesive playground. Michael and Trevor are hired by Martin Madrazo to take down a plane carrying his cousin Javier. Michael starts things off by shooting at the aircraft from Galileo Observatory with a sniper rifle.

The best part is the handoff, a seminal showcase of GTAV’s character-switch mechanic. First, Michael is coolly shooting down a plane from a mountaintop, and moments later you’re controlling Trevor, flying down country roads on a Sanchez motorcycle, chasing the falling debris like a man following his destiny. Eventually, Trevor finds Javier, kills him and climbs into the wrecked plane to retrieve the package. And, because this is Trevor, the mission ends with Trevor pining after Martin’s wife, Patricia, and kidnapping her. So much for the moral of Obsession.

When GTAIII first dropped, I spent the first few hours of the game gazing longingly across the river to Staunton Island, imagining what came next. Back in those days, Grand Theft Auto’s world opened up in stages and phases, trusting players to forgo instant gratification. That little stretch of water felt like the portal to another world entirely.

After Claude is victim of a double-cross, Maria helps him flee from Portland to Staunton where he meets his next boss, Asuka. But here’s the rub: Claude first has to prove he’s no longer the Mafia’s strongman, which means gunning down the beloved don Salvatore Leone in the heart of his turf. Once the deed is done, the Leones turn on you for the rest of the game, transforming the St. Marks neighborhood into a veritable “shotgun hell,” as YouTuber The Professional dubbed it in a video rant a few years ago. “Sayonara Salvatore” is thrilling enough. But its lasting impact on the open world is what players still can’t stop talking about.

If “Three Leaf Clover” feels familiar, that’s because it is. The mission is Rockstar’s loving homage to Michael Mann’s Heat. Niko joins Packie McReary and his brothers to rob the Bank of Liberty, complete with suits, masks, enormous bags of cash, and a getaway that quickly turns into a war through the streets of Liberty City.

There’s a little Point Break in there too: A civilian tries to play hero inside the bank, killing Michael Keane before being killed himself, echoing a similar moment in the 1991 film. Then comes the seemingly endless firefight through Algonquin’s neighborhoods, followed by an escape into the subway tunnels — the best transit system, by the way, in GTA history.

Vermeij says that in GTAIV, missions were often centered more around story than gameplay, but both are top-notch here. “These scripts could get quite big,” he said. “Thousands of lines in some cases…With every fix the script got a little more complicated.” This is GTA IV at its most cinematic, channeling the American crime movies and cop thrillers that have long shaped the series, all the while paving the way for GTAV’s slew of heists. “Four Leaf Clover,” though, remains the gold standard.

#6663. The Attico Resort 2027

There’s something rather unnerving about a woman who is always perfectly turned out. The Attico’s spring collection takes the idea of composure and gives it a mischievous twist, imagining a cast of ladies whose immaculate appearances belie rather less conventional instincts. Think The Stepford Wives relocated to Milan, where good breeding, impeccable tailoring, and a well-managed domestic interior are still considered valuable social assets. At least until someone lets her hair down.

Sharp shoulders, sculpted jackets, corseted tops, and rigorously constructed dresses establish an almost 1940s-inspired formality, with a touch of Milanese perbenismo (bourgeois respectability). But the facade, as ever at The Attico, is deceptive. Crinkled fabrics undermine the precision, lingerie details escape their appointed boundaries, and florals introduce an unlikely note of romance. Beneath the buttoned-up exterior, a streak of kink is alive and well: pencil skirts that can be unbuttoned at the sides, thigh-high slits and revealing openings that turn propriety into a rather flexible concept.

There is a more grown-up, composed attitude extending into daywear and a cleaner approach to evening, where the emphasis shifts from decorative extravagance (feathers, sequins, fringe) to cut, silhouette, and construction. Even the most restrained looks, however, seem to harbor a secret. The Attico’s perfect woman may know how to behave. Whether she chooses to is another matter.

#6662. All the Looks From The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping NYC Premiere

Including fantastical ensembles from Elle Fanning, Glenn Close, and Rachel Zegler

Are you ready to return to the Capitol? On November 20, the latest installment of the Hunger Games franchise—subtitled Sunrise on the Reaping—arrives to theaters in the United States. To celebrate the premiere, cast members old and new walked the red carpet at Alice Tully Hall in New York City on Monday evening, in what turned out to be an array of fantastical looks.

Longtime fans of the Hunger Games movies were treated to appearances from original stars like Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson, who even posed together on the carpet, sending Everlark shippers into a frenzy. Lawrence wore a silky black coat from Dior with a shearling collar and floral embroidery, while Hutcherson stepped out in a sharp black suit from Balenciaga.

And newer members of the cast pulled off equally show-stopping fits. Rachel Zegler, who starred as Lucy Gray Baird in the former Hunger Games prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, was magnificent in an emerald gown from the Zuhair Murad Fall/Winter 2026 haute couture collection.

Glenn Close embraced the avant-garde label of the moment, Matiéres Fécales, with a diaphanous black dress with a dramatic tulle train. And Elle Fanning and Elizabeth Banks each brought their own striking approaches to the character they both portray onscreen: Effie Trinket. (Fanning did so in a Givenchy by Sarah Burton dress embroidered with vintage compacts, while Banks chose a lace-up floral mermaid skirt and velvet cropped jacket from Christian Siriano.)

Ahead, take a look at all the marvelous ensembles that made their way down the red carpet at the NYC premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

In Zuhair Murad Fall/Winter 2026 haute couture.
