#6660. How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”

But embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

It’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

And so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we launched, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very quickly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We launched overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some issues we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process showed with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

Then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

That’s very well said. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really showed through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

We saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

We only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

It’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on issues “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Routine Excellence with Real Live Astronaut Reid Wiseman.”

#6659. Bond: The Business of James Bond

This week, the internet is abuzz with news of the much-anticipated casting of the new James Bond: Robert Pattinson, one of this year’s favorite leading men.

Pattinson’s arrival to the Bond franchise also marks the most luxury fashion-entrenched 007 actor yet. Pattinson has been a Dior ambassador for over 10 years, and has remained a key face for the brand since Jonathan Anderson took the helm in June last year. And in September — just two months before his Bond casting announcement — Pattinson was announced as Swiss watchmaker Jaeger-LeCoultre’s new global ambassador. The announcement generated $1 million in media impact value (MIV) within 48 hours for the brand, according to Launchmetrics.

Pattinson’s fashion affiliates were quick to stake their claim on the actor around the news of his casting. Dior’s Anderson posted an image of Pattinson and ex-Bond Daniel Craig on his personal Instagram story, taken at Anderson’s first Dior men’s 2026 show last summer, complete with a heart emoji. (Anderson had previously cast Craig in Loewe’s Fall/Winter 2024 campaign, around the same time he worked with the actor while doing the costumes for Luca Guadagnino’s Queer.) Richemont-owned Jaeger-LeCoultre, meanwhile, has posted two stills of the newly minted global ambassador to its Instagram account since Monday morning’s announcement.

Pattinson may have the most pre-existing off-screen deals of any Bond, but on-screen, the franchise is a blueprint for mega-deals between brands and movies. Partnerships have been part of the 007 world since Sean Connery stepped into the role of Bond in the inaugural Bond movie Dr. No in 1962, which featured hatmaker Lock & Co. Bond has driven an Aston Martin since 1964’s Goldfinger, Bollinger has been Bond’s champagne of choice since 1979’s Moonraker, and Heineken has been a partner since 1997. The beer brand has reportedly spent over $100 million on Bond sponsorship. Swiss watchmaker Omega is Bond’s longest-running sponsor and has decorated the wrists of Bonds since 1995, while also developing Bond watches for sale. (Prior to that, Bond wore a Rolex.) Past-era Bonds have cycled through different suit brands: Pierce Brosnan wore Brioni suits (and later starred in a campaign for the brand), as did Craig in Casino Royale. For the rest of Craig’s tenure, though, he wore Tom Ford.

The value of a Bond film has only grown. Spectre was estimated to feature $45 million in product placement; while the most recent Bond film — No Time to Die, Craig’s last — reportedly featured almost $100 million in brand placements and partnerships. In 2026, Bond’s on-screen value is immense. So much so that, last year, Amazon MGM Studios was said to have paid $20 million for the franchise, plus additional payouts that could total up to $1 billion to take full creative control over the franchise.

Brand deals have evolved dramatically since the early days of Bond — and even since the last movie. “Five years ago, an ambassadorship primarily meant red carpets and campaigns, while the film was kept separate,” says Krista Corrigan, senior retail analyst at EDITED. Now, they’re bleeding into the films themselves, whether by financially supporting films (and getting their clothes on-screen in the process), or inking deals with studios, as Dior recently did with A24. “Luxury brands give studios the aspirational quality that Bond depends on in return for a global marketing moment.”

Daniel Craig celebrating 60 years of James Bond in 2022.

The landscape into which this new Bond is releasing is dramatically different from the No Time to Die days of 2021. That was pre-Barbiecore, well before the number of brand-film-product collaborations for a given movie surpassed the hundreds, and was a different era of film promotion, before A24’s embrace of fashion and merch developed into a playbook in and of itself.

“What’s interesting about Bond is that there has always been that one iconic fashion moment or item everyone wants. Think Halle Berry’s orange bikini in Die Another Day,” says Adee Drexler, founder and CEO of communications agency ICA, who regularly brokers brand deals for clients. “These moments become part of pop culture and often live far beyond the film itself.”

The difference today, she argues, is that these moments can go viral overnight — which means the pressure to convert cultural relevance into commercial impact is heightened. “By aligning costume design, brand partnerships, and retail, the franchise can ensure that when an item captures the public’s attention, there’s already a way for consumers to buy into that moment,” Drexler says.

Will Pattinson’s be the most luxury-heavy Bond era yet? And how will the actor’s brand deals come into play?

Robert Pattinson in Dior for the Primetime screening in Venice.

Already, online chatter is bubbling about the impact of Pattinson’s current brand ambassadorships on the films. Puck’s Matt Belloni reported in his newsletter on Tuesday that Pattinson’s test deal didn’t address the actor’s current brand deals with Dior and Jaeger-LeCoultre, and that these will now need to be ironed out. One Redditor worried that Pattinson’s existing brand deals could delay filming. Most respondents expected not.

Still, it raises questions about how an actor’s off-screen brand ambassadorships influence their on-screen outfitting. “This is the first time in recent memory that a new Bond has been cast with a major luxury relationship already in place,” Corrigan says. “While brands have historically attached themselves to the role, this time it went to an actor already tied to Dior. With release expected in 2028, Dior —if involved — has plenty of time to design menswear around the film, which I’d expect to see over the next few seasons.”

Corrigan wouldn’t be surprised to see Dior on-screen come 2028, particularly given the brand’s recent embrace of the film industry and Anderson’s many costume designer credits. On November 12, Dior sent an email to US customers presenting Anderson’s cruise 2027 collection — shown in Los Angeles — as an exploration of the house’s Hollywood history, she notes.

Even if Dior isn’t integrated into the films themselves, the brand still stands to gain, Drexler says. “The press tour, premieres and cultural conversation create an enormous opportunity for Dior to own those fashion moments and translate that visibility into real commercial impact.”

Robert Pattinson in Dior, again, at the New York premiere of Die My Love.

Bond’s watch may be a different story. Jaeger-LeCoultre may have been posting Pattinson, but Omega wasted no time in staking its own claim on the Bond franchise. The brand got ahead of Pattinson’s casting by launching new models in its Seamaster diver’s watch collection, the James Bond and Spectre, in October. Omega will host an Art Basel Miami dinner to celebrate the Bond-themed timepieces. And on Tuesday morning, less than a day after Pattinson’s announcement, the watchmaker posted an image of its Seamaster Diver 300M James Bond Edition watch. Commenters were quick to pick up on what they expect to be a “battle” between the two Swiss watchmakers.

It may be a case of the highest bidder, and Omega is one of the largest watchmakers in the world (though Richemont CEO Johann Rupert recently told investors that Jaeger-LeCoultre was up 17% in the most recent quarter). Or it may be an on-screen, off-screen split. Some brand ambassadorship contracts include non-exclusivity clauses for filming. That said, when films know an actor is an ambassador for a given brand, producers will sometimes request to borrow clothing from that brand, given the existing relationship. For a moneyed franchise like Bond, though, no lending will be necessary. Instead, it’s a question of which brand will be Pattinson’s official outfitter.

Plus, for a role like Bond, the character the actor plays on-screen does become synonymous with the actor off-screen, particularly given how long the actor remains in the role. (Pattinson has a three-film deal.) One couldn’t imagine Craig donning Omega watches on-screen, while shilling non-Omega watches off-screen. In fact, the actor was — and still is — an official Omega ambassador.

Whichever brands do fill out this next iteration of the Bond world, they’ll have even more work cut out for them than in eras past, Drexler says. “It’s about moving beyond traditional product placement and creating partnerships that can capitalize on cultural moments in real time, without compromising the authenticity of the Bond universe.”

#6657. The Best Coffee-Table Books to Gift Your Beautiful, Discerning Friends

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

These books will please everyone on your gift list this year

Every year holidays come around, and a slight panic sets in at the thought of finding gifts that the people you love will get excited about—and that will make them feel seen. The real trick is to keep a list throughout the year of everything you see that reminds you of this person or that person. But because sometimes you don’t write things down because you’re “sure you’ll remember,” and because even if you do, we need all the help we can get in discovering cool things, we’ve put together a list of our favorite coffee-table books to give (and to receive, if we’re being honest) this year.

From fashion monographs to punk rock album covers to a guide to medieval wellness, we promise that we’ve found something that will thrill even your most cynical friend.

Richard Avedon was undoubtedly one of the greatest photographers of the 20th century and this collection gathers his work for Harper’s Bazaar from 1944 to 1965. As the world experienced generation-defining shifts, Avedon was zeroed in on his style, creating indelible images that would go on to change fashion. Bonus? It pairs perfectly with Ron Howard’s documentary on the photographer, also titled simply Avedon.

This massive pink tome, assembled by Coppola herself from her own collection of photographs, scripts, collages, and all manner of feminine detritus, offers a revealing and inspirational look at the director’s process and world-building.

With wit and humor, medievalist Larisa Grollemond sheds light on the way humans lived—and thrived(?)—during the middle ages. Is it true they never bathed? Did they have practice birth control? Were witches in fact, doctors? This books holds the answers.

Raymond Pettibon may now be a certified blue-chip artist, but he began his career in the 1970s drawing flyers and record covers for punk bands in Southen California like Minutemen and Black Flag. (He also designed their iconic four-bar logo, which has now been meme-fied.) This book collects his musical body of work, which also includes the Foo Fighters and Lana del Rey—that’s his work on the cover of Norman Fucking Rockwell.

The elusive Martin Margiela may very well be the designer that has most influenced contemporary fashion. Nowhere is that more evident than in this book that looks at the time when the Belgian designer was at the helm of Hermés. The enduring appeal of the collections he created from 1997 to 2002 would go on to set the tone for the whole quiet luxury moment we’ve been living under—except better.

Jeff Goodwin was the makeup artist for David Lynch’s iconic film Blue Velvet. His personal trove of Polaroid photos capture impromptu behind-the-scenes moments and reveal how he refined the makeup looks; they’re accompanied by his own memories of the filming experience.

How many people’s fashion obsessions began as they endlessly dressed and undressed their dolls—be they Barbie, Bratz, or even American Girl dolls? This tome looks at the symbiotic relationship between dolls and real-life grown-up fashion, zeroing in on the works of designers like Comme des Garçons’ Rei Kawakubo and Viktor & Rolf’s Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren, among others.

This is a book designed to inspire. For “Kitchen Piece,” Ono suggests one “hangs a canvas on a wall” and “throws all the leftovers you have” on it, with the caveat that “you may prepare special food for the piece.” After spending time with Ono’s instructions, one realizes there is art to be found literally everywhere.

This is the only book about Carolyn Bessette Kennedy that one may ever need. Sunita Kumar Nair talks to CBK’s friends and, through a carefully curated edit of images, breaks down her style. She also reveals the true essence of the person behind all those infinitely rebloggable images.

Past Continuous is the name of an exhibit at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York that brings together the world of Lee Krasner and her husband Jackson Pollock and looks at their career arcs in tandem. It begins with a selection of their paintings before the pair met, and traces their influences, taking a closer look at how their presences wove in and out of each other’s work.

This tome celebrates America’s 250th anniversary through over 200 pages filled with iconic images that have defined the country throughout its history, from images of cowboys wearing their worn-in Levi’s and immigrants landing at Ellis Island to Martin Luther King and Elvis Presley.

Diane Arbus’s unflinching photographs captured humanity in all its beautiful and exacting rawness. Documents tells the history of her short-lived career through essays, criticism, and other ephemera from 1967 through the present day; it’s a comprehensive guide to understanding her work.

Glen Luchford photographed a few of Prada’s most iconic ad campaigns of the 1990s. This book brings them all together along with alternate shots and test shots, and is an essential for both Prada aficionados and lovers of the decade.

Created in 1909 by Arthur E. Waite and Pamela Colman Smith in London, the appropriately titled Waite Smith tarot deck is the most popular deck in the world. This book looks at its history, uncovering the details and meaning of each individual card—and it comes with its own set of cards.

This year, the Fashion Museum Antwerp is celebrating its 40th anniversary with an exhibition dedicated to the “Antwerp Six,” the name the fashion media gave to a group of designers—Dries van Noten, Ann Demeulemeeter, Marina Yee, Dirk Bikkembergs, Walter Van Beirendonck, and Dirk Van Seene—that arrived in London in the mid ’80s fresh after their graduation from the Royal Academy of Fine Art. For those who can’t make it to Belgium to see the show, the book may prove to be the next best thing, chock full of photographs, illustrations, newspaper clippings, and essays. They may not have all become household names, but their influence can still be felt on the runways today.

Brianna Capozzi’s unique view of womanhood has made her one of the most sought-after photographers in fashion. Her latest monograph features a mix of magazine shots of famous singers and actors with images of impromptu shoots staged with her best friends. The result is a visual shot of adrenaline and a reminder that girls—well, women—just wanna have fun!

#6656. Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond

After a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney. There’s a new James Bond—and his name is Robert Pattinson.

The announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a new creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in February 2025, four years after No Time to Die was released. Now, Pattinson will tux up as the seventh cinematic Bond under the stewardship of super-producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal and the vision of GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, marking arguably the biggest role of the 40-year-old London-born actor’s career.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Rumors of Pattinson’s selection caught fire in October, when delays on The Batman Part II gave him a window to audition for Bond at Berkshire’s Bray Studios, alongside peers Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and an unnamed fourth actor. The chatter heightened a couple weeks later when various British tabloids suggested that Turner, O’Connor, and Lowden were each the preferred choice to satisfy the demands and responsibilities of the beloved British action hero—heightening suspicion that a final decision was looming. According to THR, the finalists were judged “based on stunts, camera presence.” But Pattinson’s last-minute arrival clearly tipped the scale.

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” said Villeneuve in a statement to THR. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

It’s both a particularly inspired and obvious choice. Pattinson’s physical traits and characteristics hue close to Ian Fleming’s original Bond—tall and slim, with dark hair. He’s already a bona fide movie star, the current face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise; meanwhile, the selection catches him at the tail end of another booked-and-busy year. Unlike his auditioning peers, the acclaimed actor will enter the franchise well-experienced working in IP and with big-name directors. After co-leading this spring’s The Drama, he chewed up scenes as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (the second time working with Nolan after Tenet), made a creepy turn as Chris Hansen in Primetime, and will close 2026 as Scytale in Dune: Part 3—now the first of future Villeneuve collaborations, a relationship that surely helped him acquire his license to kill.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” Pascal and Heyman stated jointly to THR. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

The decision to hire a movie star isn’t a risky choice, but there’s not much precedent within the franchise—especially recently. When he succeeded Pierce Brosnan as Bond in 2005, beating out Clive Owen, Michael Fassbender, and Henry Cavill, Craig boasted an under-the-radar resume. He’d just come off Matthew Vaughn’s crime thriller Layer Cake, but otherwise had played supporting roles in Road to Perdition, The Mother, and Enduring Love. His only big-budget studio experience came several years earlier as Angelina Jolie’s love interest in Tomb Raider.

Naturally, the British press drew its fangs upon his selection, critiquing everything from his general obscurity to his physical features, which stood in stark contrast to previous Bond actors. “The Mane’s Blond, James Blond,” chirped The Irish Times, while The London Daily Mirror played with the same pun: “The Name’s Bland … James Bland.” At his official introduction to the press along the Thames, Craig arrived on a speedboat wearing a life vest, attracting instant mockery—the first of several digs about his less-than-sleek aesthetic and physical abilities. (One tabloid insulted an on-set sunburn and his inability to drive a stick shift car.)

Pattinson, however, has mostly conjured genuine excitement—not in spite of, but because of, his extreme familiarity with moviegoers, dating back to his Young Adult days in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises. Since then, over the last decade-plus, his eccentric characters and commanding screen presence immediately qualifies him as someone “stirring and exciting and different,” descriptors that Pascal said she prioritized in their methodical search.

Thanks to director Martin Campbell, Casino Royale returned the Bond franchise to earth and established Craig as a grounded, gritty action star in the mold of Jason Bourne. The movie ended up raking in $616 million globally, the highest earning Bond film to date, and launched Craig into four more sequels. Similarly, Pattinson will have the benefit of a highly-respected, Oscar-nominated director in his corner with experience shepherding IP into new places and eliciting compelling performances about tortured male protagonists.

With Villeneuve at the helm of this 26th installment, don’t expect another hard creative pivot; the man behind Prisoners, Blade Runner 2049, and Dune wasn’t hired to bring back the colorful, absurdist, gadget-heavy era that Austin Powers parodied throughout the 90’s. Still, new leadership means a new direction—a clean slate for Pattinson to burnish an already diverse, robust career and prove his chops again at the highest level of scrutiny.

#6655. Jennifer Lawrence Has Her Swan Moment With a New It-Bag

Jennifer Lawrence knows better than to let a serious event or outfit get in the way of a very unserious handbag. At WWD’s 2026 Beauty Inc Awards in New York on Tuesday evening, the Hunger Games and beauty founder arrived in a sculptural black Dior tuxedo jacket, with exaggerated hips and lapels and a frothy, feathered ivory miniskirt. So far, so classic red carpet.

Her choice of accessory—plucked from her already enviable suite of it-bags—certainly made a statement. Lawrence toted the Dior Cygnet Minaudière, a miniature swan-shaped clutch from Jonathan Anderson’s spring 2027 collection—an objet d’art with a wink, and one Anderson has certainly become known for. The designer has form when it comes to feathered friends: recall the infamous pigeon clutch from his eponymous label.

Lawrence was clearly quite taken with her new companion. Earlier that day, she carried the same swan to Beauty Inc’s The Catalysts, where she appeared on stage alongside Jasmina Aganovic, her partner in the recently launched haircare brand mes°. For that engagement, she paired a fluffy white longline cardigan with a simple tank top, relaxed blue jeans, and heels, adding CompletedWorks onyx drop earrings. By evening, the bird had spread its wines to experience the full red-carpet glamour it deserves, accompanied by antique Fred Leighton diamond earrings and black satin Jimmy Choo mules.

J Law’s handbag collection is already the stuff of fantasy. There are the serious investments—Hermès Kellys, Loewe Puzzles, and Phoebe Philo’s Gig bag—but increasingly, she’s making room for accessories with a little more personality. Consider her leopard-print Prada Galleria, complete with brightly colored ostrich leather accents, or her see-through Gimaguas baguette. The swan is a natural addition to the family.

And the same taste for the fantastical is extending to her outerwear. After the awards, Lawrence emerged in a sumptuous red velvet jacket, carrying another Dior bag: a fuzzy black DiorAlps shearling tote. It joins an increasingly fabulous rotation of novelty coats, from her dramatic fur-trimmed Dior coatdress to the chartreuse Colleen Allen housecoat she recently took out with a pair of slippers.

Jennifer Lawrence may have mastered the art of understated yet expensive-looking dressing, but she’s never lost her appetite for something a little cheeky. Take flight!

#6652. Anne Hathaway Gives Birth to Her Third Child

Congratulations are in order for Anne Hathaway! The actor has welcomed her third child with husband Adam Shulman, making them a family of five.

On Tuesday, November 17, Hathaway was photographed out and about in New York City with a newborn nestled against her chest in a baby carrier. People has since independently confirmed the happy news. The baby’s name, sex, and exact birth date have not yet been shared.

Hathaway and Shulman, who married in 2012, are already parents to two boys: Jonathan, 10, and Jack, who was born in November 2019. The couple have largely kept their children out of the public eye.

The Oscar winner first announced her third pregnancy in June, with a sweet Instagram video soundtracked by Barbara Lewis’s “Baby I’m Yours.” Wearing a flowing white linen two-piece by Nothing Fits But and gold-embellished Cult Gaia sandals, Hathaway walked into the frame, revealed her growing bump, beamed at the camera, and ran playfully out of sight. “x Baby, I’m yours x,” she captioned the post. During an appearance on Late Night With Seth Meyers the following month, she affectionately referred to the surprise addition as the couple’s “buzzer-beater” baby.

It’s been a pregnancy style journey for Annie. Working with stylist Erin Walsh, Hathaway delivered some of the year’s most memorable maternity looks: goddess-like custom Dior and Prada gowns on The Odyssey press tour, as well as more playful, bump-baring separates, and an ethereal lilac Alexander McQueen dress during New York Fashion Week. She rounded out her run of red carpets at the Verity premiere in September, wearing a dramatic black sequined tulle Prabal Gurung gown.

Indeed, if anyone has earned a little downtime, it’s Anne Hathaway. The actor has had an extraordinarily busy 2026, with five films released this year alone: Mother Mary, The Devil Wears Prada 2, The Odyssey, The End of Oak Street, and Verity. Between reprising her beloved role as Andy Sachs, playing Penelope in Christopher Nolan’s Greek epic, and diving deep into Colleen Hoover’s much hyped psychological thriller, Hathaway has scarcely stopped the promo tour.

But now, she’s looking forward to some time away from the spotlight. Speaking to Vogue at the Verity premiere, Hathaway shared that her favorite moment of the entire year had been discovering she was pregnant, and the forthcoming opportunity to take a pause. “I’m really excited to meet my baby, and to be in that little bubble in time,” she said.

Five films plus a fabulous maternity wardrobe, and a new baby. Congratulations once again to Anne Hathaway and Adam Schulman!

#6651. Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Announcement Is Already Brewing Some Watch Drama

Throughout the years-long process of casting the new James Bond, I tried to follow the watches to an answer. When Aaron Taylor-Johnson joined the Omega family in May 2025, it felt like watching the 007 Vatican spit white smoke from its steeple. Just this past weekend, fans were still pinning red strings on their bulletin boards between Jack Lowden and the MI6 superspy when images resurfaced of the Slow Horses star wearing Omega. Since 1995’s Goldeneye, Bond has been an Omega man—a relationship later canonized in one of cinema’s most iconic line readings, when Daniel Craig confirmed his brand of choice in three stretched-out syllables: Oh-Mee-Guh.

If, like me, you were only basing your predictions on what the reported pool of potential Bonds wore on their wrists, Robert Pattinson would have been an easy name to cross off. The newly announced 007 only signed on as an ambassador for the Swiss luxury brand Jaeger-LeCoultre two short months ago! When I interviewed Pattinson about the appointment over the summer, he was effusive about his new partner: “I very rarely even wear watches, but when I tried it on, I was like, ‘That’s my favorite watch.’ I wanted to just buy it.”

Now, in addition to juggling his other iconic role as Batman, Pattinson will presumably need to balance his existing commitment to JLC with his new gig’s long-held ties to Omega. (Reps for both brands did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though JLC conspicuously posted a photo of Pattinson on Instagram a few hours after the announcement.)

During our conversation earlier this summer, Pattinson revealed what he looks for in a watch. He caught the collecting bug in March, when he wore JLC’s Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar to the Oscars afterparties. “All these other actors with their fancy watches on asked me, ‘Hey, what are you wearing?’” Pattinson recalls. “It was one of those moments where I’m like, ‘It’s kind of badass having this thing on.’”

If it’s attention-grabbing badass watches Pattinson is after, he’s in good hands with Omega. The brand is best known for supplying the watches Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin wore when they landed on the moon in 1969. Omega has been happy to create special versions of the Speedmaster for its current partners to dial up its profile. And, of course, the Swiss house continues to expand its Bond-inspired offerings: The maker recently added a “Spectre” version of the Seamaster, 007’s preferred model, to the lineup. And whenever Omega needs to drum up buzz around soon-to-be-released models, they tend to show up on former Bond Craig’s wrists during public appearances.

Speculators trying to pin down the next Bond would have had better luck if they’d read some less recent watch tea leaves. Back in 2020, Christopher Nolan released Tenet, his inscrutable but enthralling time-warp thriller in which Pattinson plays a mysterious, dapper, and charming spy involved in a high-stakes mission to save the world—about as good a preview of what the 40-year-old actor will look like as 007 as you’ll find in his filmography. And the watch on his wrist in that flick? An Omega.

#6648. David Duchovny on Books, Band and ‘The X-Files’

David Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”

Duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he says of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”

I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he says. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”)

The albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny says—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, says.

At 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”

For the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucky Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”

“Good question,” Duchovny says, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”

Inevitably, someone asks about the new X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has plans, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he says, “I know he said he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”

Duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he said: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”

Duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He says, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”

In college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He showed up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”

The two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play a character inspired by paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a film that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”

I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he says.

In LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he said on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron said.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny said, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”

Truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons said no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he says. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I said: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”

I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he says. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”

“It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

“Lower than zero,” Duchovny says. “Less than zero.”

A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”

#6645. Hunter Schafer’s Peekaboo Ponytail Is the Cool Girl’s Red Carpet Look

From intricate braids and gravity-defying knots to elaborate, architectural chignons, the red carpet has seen plenty of sculptural hair looks as of late. Leave it to Hunter Schafer to offer a decidedly cool-girl interpretation of the trend.

Attending the London premiere of Blade Runner 2099 on Tuesday evening, Schafer—styled as always by Dara—wore a custom ivory Celine ensemble comprising a strapless satin bustier dress, with a dramatic train trailing behind her, layered over tailored tuxedo trousers for that nonchalant elegance. Her beauty followed suit. Working with her go-to hairstylist Rena Calhoun, Schafer wore her honey-blonde lengths in softly tousled, loose waves, parted loosely at the center and falling around her shoulders. From the front it was a classic and romantic, and a rather effortless-looking hairstyle. But turn around, and there was a delightful little surprise: a tiny, twisted, extremely low ponytail woven into the ends of her hair at the nape of her neck, secured with a wrap of blonde strands. The mini braid was a lovely, blink-and-you’ll-miss-it detail. Makeup artist Sandy Ganzer kept things similarly soft, with subtly defined eyes, flushed cheeks, and a rosy pink lip.

It’s another clever beauty moment in what’s proving to be an excellent press tour for Schafer. At the Los Angeles premiere last week, Ganzer paid homage to Daryl Hannah’s replicant character Pris in Ridley Scott’s original Blade Runner, creating a dramatic, futuristic strip of gunmetal eyeshadow across her eyes and nose. Calhoun fashioned her hair into a disheveled updo, with flyaways escaping at the back for a cyberpunk heroine to red carpet look.

Then there were the hair-matching fuzzy earmuffs from Undercover’s fall 2007 collection, which Calhoun incorporated into a double-ponytail hairstyle. Working alongside Dara and Ganzer, Schafer has been having enormous fun with beauty references that are both deeply considered and playful, often drawing on the sci-fi world of her forthcoming series and beyond.

The up-do renaissance is firmly upon us. At this year’s Golden Globes, Audrey Nuna, Mia Goth, and Jenna Ortega were among those experimenting with interesting shapes and structures, while Anya Taylor-Joy recently sported a sleek knot at the LACMA Art+Film Gala.

What’s so great about Hunter Schafer’s latest look is its restraint. While everyone else is twisting, sculpting, and shellacking their hair into elaborate works of art, Schafer makes a case for something more low-key. Sometimes the most interesting beauty detail is the one you almost miss.

#6644. Robert Pattinson Might Be the Most Fashion-Forward Bond Yet

From Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr. No to Daniel Craig’s thigh-bearing trunks in Casino Royale, each man who has played James Bond has brought a new aesthetic sensibility to the role. For Connery, this meant soft-shouldered Savile Row tailoring, polo shirts, and knit ties to suit the era of Ivy Style, while Roger Moore’s wardrobe of safari jackets and nylon ski suits embodied the sporty hedonism of the 1970s. In the 21st century, Daniel Craig’s Bond was built around a timely blend of Brioni, Tom Ford, and stalwart British brands that complemented the contemporary #menswear scene. Today’s news that Robert Pattinson—a longtime Dior ambassador and one of the most consistently thrilling dressers in Hollywood—has been cast as 007 suggests Bond’s most fashionable era may be yet to come.

Daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops. Pattinson, meanwhile, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for a decade, during which he’s established his impeccable taste and a willingness to take big swings with his outfits—not to mention a reputation for wearing the absolute heck out of a gray suit. Now, with fellow Brit Jonathan Anderson (who cast Craig in Loewe’s quirked-up fall 2024 campaign and posted this heartwarming pic today) running the show at Dior, the stage is set for a Bond with a taste for capital-F fashion.

Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a new Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear. Pierce Brosnan’s era had structured Brioni suits and made the Omega Seamaster a star, while Daniel Craig helped cement Tom Ford’s tailoring as a red-carpet staple and juiced sales of N.Peal ribbed Army sweaters and Drake’s suede chukkas. As GQ’s Cam Wolf noted in a 2018 article about Skyfall, Daniel Craig’s Barbour jacket, sweater, jeans, and brogue boots from that film—a classic but fairly unremarkable outfit—became the aspirational template for untold numbers of men on r/malefashionadvice. A few years later, when Craig wore a Rag & Bone slim-fit henley in No Time to Die, the brand sold out of the unassuming undershirt in a matter of days.

It’s been five years since No Time to Die’s release, and it will likely be at least a couple more before Pattinson’s first outing as 007 hits screens. That’s a long wait to see how the next Bond era aesthetic comes together, but given Pattinson’s distinctive approach to fashion, it should be well worth it for the clothes alone.

#6642. Shopbop’s Collab With Julia Berolzheimer Is Even Better Than We’d Hoped

Consider it a smash hit among fashion editors.

As you might imagine, my coworkers and I, well, we see a crap ton of clothes on a daily basis. We’re fashion editors, after all. Our working hours are spent poring over the latest collections, visiting showrooms to experience the pieces for ourselves, and analyzing every trend. All that said, we can be a tough bunch to impress. I mean that earnestly. But when my colleague and I saw a sneak preview of the collaboration between Shopbop’s in-house label, Le Bop, and Julia Berolzheimer, we nearly squealed with delight.

The collection hits all the right notes. It’s colorful. It’s fun yet sophisticated. And for Berolzheimer, the collaboration felt like a full-circle moment. “I have been a customer of Shopbop since the very beginning of my blog (15 years ago!),” Berolzheimer exclusively told ELLE in an email. “Even back then, Shopbop was a destination for style inspiration and discovery...All of that still holds true for the retailer today. When their design team reached out to me last year to co-design a collection for their private label, Le Bop, it was a no-brainer.”

The collection features taffeta and satiny fabrics adorned with fringe, tonal animal prints, brocade jackets, and jacquard knits. The rich color palette includes dusty rose, chartreuse, espresso, and ocean blue. It is, I must admit, perfect for party dressing that feels a bit unexpected.

“The inspiration came naturally,” Berolzheimer says. “It stemmed from my personal style and what I love and want to wear around the holidays. I call my style ‘polished maximalist,’ and the collection is just that. There are some bold statement pieces and coordinating sets, which I love to style together, but you can also wear them separately for a more pared-down look. What I love most about this collection is how you can mix and match the pieces for any festive occasion and continue to style them beyond the holiday season.”

The Le Bop x Julia Berolzheimer collection is available now on Shopbop.com.

#6641. The 15 Best Airbnbs in the Alps, Whether You’re an Avid Skier or Just in it for the Après

We are headed right into the thick of ski season; when warm, wool knitwear is the uniform du jour, and the temperature is the kind of cold that’s completely inexcusable unless accompanied by plates of melty raclette at après-ski. This is your sign to book your winter getaway in advance. And while there are tons of great ski resorts you could jet off to, nothing quite beats an Alpine retreat—whether freeskiing in Zermatt or trialing bunny slopes in Megève, you have options. The best Airbnbs in the Alps, from Austria to France to Italy, are the perfect place to stay if you need more flexibility and space than a hotel.

It’s a vast region—the Dolomites alone are an 18-peak range—so there’s a lot to choose from. Go for stately chalet elegance with a multi-bedroom option if you’re traveling with lots of friends and family; book something closer to a cozy cabin if you prefer a low-key holiday. These 15 options span the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps, as well as a range of prices and styles. Your next decision? Which Fair Isle sweater will make it into your carry-on.

Those in search of the most traditional of Alpine vacations will find everything they’re looking for in this peaceful chalet—right down to the Savoyard pottery. It looks out onto the Aravis mountains, just five minutes away from the Croix-Fry ski resort and 40 minutes from the busier spots of Annecy and Megève. It has a wood-burning fireplace that’s ideal for relaxing after a day on the slopes, and a spacious balcony for those brave enough to wrap up and take their coffee outdoors in the winter chill.

Situate yourself in the heart of one of the most sought-after ski resorts, close to all of Gstaad’s main shops. The apartment, which can sleep up to six, has heated underground parking and a ski cellar to facilitate winter trips. The interior is simple but well-appointed—the dining table being a major plus for cozy dinners—but the real draw is the balcony. Head outside for gorgeous mountain views whenever you want them.

If you’re not looking for a fully remote stay, this charming mini-chalet gives you a taste of quaint mountain village life. Renovated in 2024, the updated amenities list includes a pizza stone oven, walk-in shower, and hypoallergenic bedding. (Your booking also comes with a Beatenberg guest card, a perk inclusive of a free bus pass for travel back and forth to Interlaken for when you want to explore the alpine area.) This has all the cozy touches you’ll want for a weeklong vacation, plus one important extra: The wraparound balcony has storybook views of both Lake Thun and the Eiger, Mönch, and Jungfrau peaks.

Not all alpine retreats are stuffy, rustic cabins; some are luxurious, light-filled homes that expertly blend old and new. This spot is a perfect example. The 18th-century farmhouse right in the historic center square of Scuol was recently restored, keeping its old-world charms (that wood paneling!) while making some necessary updates. Sleek chrome furniture, a chef-grade kitchen, and whitewashed walls bring light in.

There’s no television in this mountainside cabin; all the better to truly unwind with. Instead, occupy yourself with a forest hike or a day on the slopes (the Airbnb is in the La Tzoumaz resort, by Verbier in the Swiss Alps). Wind down by candlelight, whether that’s with a warm meal served family-style at the dining table overlooking the tall trees or a game of Hearts by the fire.

It’s pretty hard to beat these views. This restored barn looks out onto Mount Pelmo in the Dolomites, with a key highlight being the covered balcony; you’ll want to take every meal there to soak in the mountain views. It can fit up to seven guests—great for a large family or group—and you’ll each have plenty of space to stretch out in.

This charming cottage in the Valais town of Ayer puts you right near all the top ski resorts: Grimentz, Zinal, St-Luc, and Chandolin are all about a 15-minute drive away. The combined dining-living space is charming, with windows that look out onto snowy hills in the winter and green pastures (plus the occasional cow) in the summer. Four bedrooms offers plenty of space for a big friend trip.

From the outside, surrounded by snowy pine trees, this chalet looks like a fairytale cottage; inside, it’s outfitted with all the contemporary amenities to make your stay a luxurious one. A Bose Bluetooth sound system, HDTV with all the streamers, and state-of-the-art kitchen appliances bring a modern element to the wood cabin. A private sauna and hot tub only add to the five-star feel.

It’s an easy drive to the alpine lake and mountains of the Salzkammergut region from this Airbnb, which sits on a spacious property surrounded by forest. Sweat out the day in the sauna or gather around the fireplace to listen to a vinyl or play a board game—both are provided by the host.

With Montblanc in the distance, this 19th-century cottage offers picturesque views from the balcony. Take your morning coffee there before heading out to the slopes or nearby hiking trails, returning home to soak in the tub, whip up a home-cooked meal, or crack open a new book in the glass-walled (and, crucially, heated) reading room.

Expect charm at every turn with this farmhouse, which dates back to the 15th century. Located in the Kaiser Mountains of the Eastern Alps, this sprawling property features wooden ceilings, terracotta tiled floors (with partial underfloor heating), and beautiful murals painted throughout—there’s even an original stove in the dining room.

This rustic mountain hut located in a secluded part of the Italian alps is actually a working farm and apiary: Those with a fear of bees, plan accordingly. A breakfast basket is provided each morning, with the freshest of ingredients you can enjoy outdoors or in the open-air kitchen in the warmer months, or by the fire in the winter. You’ll need a car to access the property—it is properly remote—but its isolation is part of the charm.

This French Alps home is ideally built for family holidays. Child-friendly features, from a travel crib to fireplace grates, will make your stay more comfortable; several separate bathrooms give everyone their own space; upscale amenities, like heated flooring and optional catering, make every day feel like a treat. It’s just south of Lake Geneva, if you want to rent a car and take a little day trip.

This apartment in the Dolomites is deceptively spacious: It sleeps up to six, with soaring A-frame ceilings giving the illusion of even more space. The theme appears to be, simply, wood. From the exposed beams to the built-in furniture to the floor-to-ceiling cupboards, the whole space is designed with rustic cabins on the brain.
