#6613. Grace Cacciato Wins the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final

After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final. A panel of judges selected her roasted squab with chanterelle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat, black raspberry, and Swiss chard purées to represent the United States at the Grand Finale in Milan.

The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City on Monday, and the winner was announced the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024–25 US winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, DC, and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

Saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he said. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

The chefs had five hours to prepare and execute their signature dishes in the Test Kitchen. With an hour remaining, guests had the opportunity to mingle over food and drinks. Chef Rachel Bindel, a 2022 US Finalist, served rye toast piled high with Maryland blue crab, horseradish crème, and pickled green tomato. Chef Akshay Kumar, a 2024 finalist, tucked Kumamoto oysters into a pani puri with cucumber gel and lemon foam. Tomato pie from Philadelphia’s Pizza Freak Co., spoonfuls of Petrossian caviar, and a selection of wines, S.Pellegrino beverages, and cocktails rounded out the reception.

Nilou Motamed, a culinary expert and Iron Chef judge on Netflix, hosted the competition. Accomplished chefs from several states served as judges: chef and co-owner E.J. Lagasse of Emeril’s in New Orleans; executive chef and partner Fariyal Abdullahi of Hav & Mar in New York City; Isabel Coss, executive chef at Pascual and founding pastry chef at Lutèce in Washington, DC; Jon Yao, head chef and owner at Kato in Los Angeles; and Ryan Ratino, executive chef and owner at Bresca and Jônt in Washington, DC.

Motamed explained that each competitor had spent several months developing their dish alongside a chef mentor. The mentors were in the Test Kitchen throughout the competition, but were not permitted to participate in the cooking. She also outlined the three pillars of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy: Community, Competition, and Mentorship, which support its mission to discover and nurture the next generation of culinary talent.

Each chef’s arrival was announced by a burst of music and a live video feed from the Test Kitchen, where a fleet of servers collected the finished plates before delivering them to the judges. First up was chef Adolfo Pucci of Michelin-starred Ariete in Miami. His dish, “Three Shores, One Table,” told the story of his Venezuelan heritage, his family’s roots in Southern Italy, and his current home in Miami. The ambitious plate featured a lamb ragù inspired by his grandmother’s cooking and lacto-fermented Florida blueberries.

Chef Amit Kumar of three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park in New York City presented the competition’s only fully vegan dish: “Sunchoke with Banana Blossoms, Chanterelles, and Sherry.” Drawing on memories of the banana trees he grew up with in India, Kumar combined banana blossoms, sunchoke purée, chanterelle mushrooms, and a ragù of sherry and banana flowers to create a hearty and deeply satisfying dish. Judge Fariyal Abdullahi called it “a very successful dish, not just a very successful vegan dish.”

Representing Auro at Four Seasons Resort and Residences Napa Valley, chef Evan Neumann presented “From the Valley to the Shoreline,” a love letter to the terroir of Northern California and Provence, where he grew up. Kombu-poached wild razor clams mingled with Napa verjuice and coastal seaweeds in a dish the judges found exceptionally creative. Neumann took home the S.Pellegrino Social Responsibility Award for his thoughtful approach to social responsibility and sustainable practices.

At just 21, chef Lucy Field of New York City’s fine dining bastion Per Se was the youngest competitor. Her dish, “Pekin Duck, Cherry, Plum,” was a study in restraint with only six components.

Chef Marcus Osorio, chef de cuisine at Living Room in Los Angeles, drew inspiration from his Salvadoran and Indigenous roots for his “Tamal de Pollo.” The dish featured corn sourced from Somos Maíz, the company founded by his mentor, chef Ron Oliver, and a mole poblano the two developed together. Judge Isabel Coss noted the challenge of preparing a mole with such limited time, but the judges were impressed by Osorio’s ability to marry European cooking techniques with soulful Indigenous ingredients and flavors.

Chef Nickolas Abbott hails from the small Appalachian town of Waynesville, North Carolina, and leads Chop Shop Butchery in Asheville. At the competition, he told the story of his community on a plate. His “Smoked Pork Loin, Fennel & Cheese Slaw, Sweet Potato, Asparagus, Fried Sausage, Pork Sauce Robert” reflected the people who shaped him, particularly his grandmother, his greatest inspiration as a chef.

Los Angeles–based chef Natasha Daniels of Providence showcased her vegetable-forward, zero-waste approach with “The Whole Bird, The Whole Garden.” The dish incorporated every part of a chicken across four preparations, alongside an array of vegetables and herbs inspired by her time working at The Chef’s Garden.

Daniels received two honors: the Acqua Panna Connection in Gastronomy Award and the Fine Dining Lovers Award. Voted on by regional mentors, the Acqua Panna award recognized the dish that best demonstrated a connection between culinary traditions. Daniels’s approach also resonated with Fine Dining Lovers insiders, who selected her for their award that honors “a chef’s expression of personal belief.”

With only minutes to spare, chef Nicolas Lopez of 888 in Nashville arrived with “Pozole or Chawanmushi…?” Combining pozole, corn, and langoustine, Lopez connected his upbringing in Mexico with a culinary journey that has been shaped by Scandinavian ingredients and Japanese techniques. Although the judges could have used more time to explore the dish, they were intrigued by his influences and impressed by his technique.

The final competitor, Juwon Lee, is the chef of Octavia in San Francisco. Lee was born in South Korea and grew up in Singapore before making California his home. His dish, “Curry and Quail with Ingredients My Mother Said Were Healthy,” drew on memories of eating Indonesian fried chicken and his mother’s insistence on including vegetables at family dinners. “I believe in the term happy food,” Lee explained. “There are no restrictions other than bringing joy to the eater and the chef.”

Congratulations to all 10 chefs who competed, and best of luck to Chef Cacciato as she continues to work with her mentor and prepares to represent the United States at the 2027 Grand Finale in Milan. Follow her journey at @sanpellegrino_us.

#6612. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6611. Vogue’s 16 Best Hotels in the Alps, From Chic Chalets to Design-Forward Boutique Stays

The Alps have a particular hold on the imagination. There are the snow-dusted peaks, naturally, and the villages tucked into their folds, with timber chalets, candlelit restaurants, and views that could make even the most committed city dweller reconsider their priorities. But the pleasures of an Alpine escape extend well beyond a day on the slopes and unlimited raclette.

Across France and Switzerland, the region’s hotels run the gamut from storied grand dames and old-world mountain inns to contemporary retreats where thoughtful architecture and considered design take center stage. Some trade in old-school glamour, others in rustic charm or a welcome degree of seclusion, but the best are worth giving up a powder morning for and staying in. Whether you’re here for serious skiing, fireside dinners, or simply the pleasure of waking up to a panorama of peaks, these are the Alpine hotels in France and Switzerland worth planning a trip around this winter.

Les Fermes de Marie, a hamlet above Megève, was put together in 1989 by Jean-Louis and Jocelyne Sibuet from Savoyard farm buildings dismantled elsewhere and carted here, stone by stone. The result is a welcome abundance of old timber, antiques, wool, plaid, and animal skins, with fires burning in the appropriate places. (The Sibuets also run La Bastide de Marie in the Luberon and Villa Marie in Saint-Tropez, but this is their grande dame; no small thing from a family this good at hospitality, especially where children are concerned.) Here, they are dispatched to Le Hameau des Enfants, a free club with its own children’s concierge, where 5-to-10-year-olds are kept busy with cooking and ski lessons.

Breakfast, served in the heart of the hotel, in the main restaurant with an enormous fireplace, is not to be slept through (on the menu: homemade jams, Alpine cheeses, farm butter, and exceptional bread). From 2 to 6 p.m. the lounges and library put out homemade Savoie cakes, whipped-cream waffles and the house hot chocolate, after which the bar moves on to wine with slates of local cheese and charcuterie. By evening the main dining room settles into traditional Savoyard cooking by the fire, including a house pâté that has earned its permanent place on the menu. Downstairs, the hotel’s stube is given over entirely to cheese—fondue included—though for dinner in town, the family also owns Le Vieux Megève, a Savoyard institution in the village with as many locals at its tables as guests. The spa’s outdoor hot tubs are best used in falling snow, when the hamlet looks sealed inside a snow globe, and the terraces come heaped with sheepskins and blankets for an evening apéritif under the heat lamps.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pool, kids’ club, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Editor’s tip: Stop by L’Épicerie de Megève, the Sibuets’ grocery in the village. The breakfast jams are on the shelves, as is honey from the hotel’s own hives and wine from the family’s Luberon estate, all of which makes for a perfect souvenir.

Address: 163 Chemin des épis, 74120 Megève

The Saint-Georges is the latest addition to Megève’s hospitality scene. Located right in the center of Megève, a few steps from the pedestrian rue Charles Feige and a short walk from the lifts, the old building has been reimagined by the English designer Luke Edward Hall as a kind of Alpine fairy tale, complete with all the decorative flourishes that the genre demands.

Savoyard folklore provided the starting point, but the 29 rooms take the idea in a cheerfully eccentric direction: Pierre Frey fabrics, painted and patterned headboards, boldly colored bathrooms, floral tiles, deep carpets, and hand-painted murals jostle against carved wood and antiques. On weekend evenings, there’s live piano beside the fire in the bar, lending the place the air of an old mountain inn in which one might reasonably expect a wolf, a princess, or at least a particularly off-kilter uncle to appear before dinner. Le Trappeur, the hotel’s bistro, serves classic French cooking with a few Savoyard dishes, while the spa takes a more elemental approach, built around hot and cold contrast therapy. Families are well catered to, with dedicated rooms and activities for children who may find themselves rather more at home here than in the usual hushed Alpine palace.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bar, kids’ club

Address: 159, Rue Monseigneur Conseil, 74120 Megève

Le Coucou occupies a large wooden chalet on Méribel’s Belvédère, beside the Rond-Point des Pistes, arranged so that the windows look out over the slopes and a blue run begins just beyond the ski room. It is ski-in, ski-out in the fullest sense: Staff are on hand to unbuckle your boots, lest the final indignity of the day prove too much.

On arrival, one encounters a domed ceiling painted by Matthieu Cossé with owls perched among trees against blue mountain peaks, which establishes the level of seriousness with which the decor is to be taken. Pierre Yovanovitch designed more than 130 pieces of furniture and lighting for the 55 rooms and public spaces—including teddy-shaped armchairs—and set them among terracotta walls, sheepskin, and upwards of 160 artworks, Calder and Chillida included. The bar, done up in yellow, blue, and cream, looks directly onto the pistes through floor-to-ceiling windows. There are indoor and outdoor pools, a Tata Harper spa, and two children’s clubs, should the adults require a little peace. For dinner, Biancaneve serves Italian food; Le Fumoir seats sixteen around a fireplace for fondue; their flagship restaurant Beefbar extends onto a terrace. The whole enterprise is unapologetically theatrical; and though one might reasonably ask how much theater a ski holiday requires, the answer, apparently, is quite a lot.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, bar, pools, kids’ clubs, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental

Address: 464 Route du Belvédère 73550 Les Allues Méribel

Courchevel has never been short of hotels willing to make a spectacle of luxury. Saint Roch, opening in December on the Bellecôte piste, is Maisons Pariente’s case for the opposite approach, one the family already made persuasively in Paris with Le Grand Mazarin and Méribel’s Le Coucou. Architects Virginie Friedmann and Delphine Versace have recast a longstanding hotel as something closer to a well-traveled aesthete’s chalet, its 37 rooms dressed in dark wood, mohair velvet, agate and onyx by way of Russian dachas and Persian interiors. Pierre Mesguich’s mosaic frescoes and Atelier Toporkoff’s stained glass do more for the place than any amount of gilt would. The living room alone, with its deep sofas and fireplace, makes a decent case for skipping the afternoon session.

Come evening, visit Prunier, the Parisian caviar house’s first alpine restaurant. To unwind further, head downstairs, where you’ll find a ceramic-tiled pool and Tata Harper treatments that take their cue from Ottoman hammams.

Amenities: Spa, pool, ski shop, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental

Address: Piste de Bellecote, 73120 Courchevel 1850

Opening in December from Chapitre Six, the group behind Megève’s Saint-Georges, Bourbon Hotel seems to have concluded that the last thing the resort needs is another chalet. Instead, it takes its cues from a London members’ club, with dark woods, deep velvets, and low lighting. It sits in Courchevel’s Golden Triangle, with direct ski-in, ski-out access to Les Trois Vallées, which is useful, though the more interesting offerings involve what happens after a day on the slopes.

Simonetta, the hotel’s Italian restaurant, will be led by Simone Zanoni, whose Paris credentials include Le George at the George V; this will be his first restaurant in the mountains. The bar pairs cocktails with vinyl sessions, a combination that suggests the après-ski hours here are to be taken at least as seriously as the skiing itself. Below ground, a spa built around contrast therapy offers the usual opportunity to repair the damage before heading out to do it all again. There are 28 rooms and three suites, and pets are permitted on request. Whether Bourbon can make the London-club formula work at altitude remains to be seen, but it is at least a departure from the expected wood-and-antler routine.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bar, ski-in, ski-out

Address: 286 Rue Park City, 73120 Courchevel

Les Airelles occupies the Place de Neige, where the village meets the mountain, with direct access to the pistes and the Solaise and Olympique gondolas, as well as a large sun terrace for watching skiers descend. Its 41 rooms, suites, and penthouses have been conceived in the spirit of a medieval Alpine residence, furnished with antiques and artworks drawn from a collection of more than 4,000 pieces. Each has a balcony or terrace, and the penthouses come with their own butler. The Bernard Orcel ski room takes care of the business of getting dressed for the mountain, and, on one’s return, offers hot drinks and crêpes. Dinner can be had at Matsuhisa or Palladio, followed by a stint in the Guerlain spa—the largest in Val d’Isère–or the private cinema.

Children have a grotto-like pool of their own, while dogs receive monogrammed mats, personalized collars, and a dedicated walker to take them out while their owners ski. There is something delightfully over-the-top about a hotel that provides more elaborate arrangements for a dog’s afternoon than most people make for their own, but Les Airelles has never been especially interested in the modest pleasures of Alpine life. Its particular talent is to turn every practical inconvenience into an occasion for service, and every stay into a small performance of aristocratic excess.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pools, cinema, ski-in, ski-out, on-site ski rental

Address: 145 Rue de la Poste, 73150 Val d'Isère

The skiing is serious in Verbier, but so is the après. Experimental, the Paris group that built its reputation on cocktail bars, chose its first Alpine hotel accordingly, opening a chalet a short walk from the lifts and directly above Farm Club; otherwise known as the nightclub that has kept the village awake since 1971.

For those who have come to ski, the village shop Les Ruinettes delivers rentals to heated lockers downstairs, and a shuttle takes guests to the lifts. The 39 rooms, designed by Fabrizio Casiraghi, favor warm wood, deep colors, and clean lines over the typical heavy chalet style. This ethos extends to the food: Saint Bernard, the restaurant beside reception, gives Alpine classics a lighter touch. Upstairs, the Experimental Cocktail Club draws a mixture of hotel guests and outsiders, while the outdoor hot tub at the Biologique Recherche spa looks directly into the bar, allowing one to order a cocktail through the window without ever getting out of the tub. Starting this November, the bar is introducing a vinyl listening room built around Klipsch speakers, where record selectors stand in for the usual resort DJ.

Amenities: Spa, restaurant, bars, nightclub, hot tub, ski lockers, shuttle

Editor’s tip: On certain weeknights, guests can bring their own records to play in the new listening bar.

Address: Route de Verbier Station 55, 1936 Verbier

Welsh brothers Grant and Craig Maunder, who have been part of Adelboden since Grant first came here in the late seventies, own two hotels in the village; the Brecon, named for the Brecon Beacons, is the smaller, quieter one, housed in a timber building dating to 1914 at the more peaceful end of town. Its interiors look to the ’50s and ’60s, with leather, wool, stone, and crazy-paved Welsh slate underfoot. (Continuing the nod to the owners’ home, you’ll also find Welsh wool blankets lie folded on the beds.)

Each of the 18 rooms and four lofts are television-free; a decision that might once have seemed a little severe but becomes easier to defend when you realize the Adelboden massif occupying the entire window offers a much better thing to stare at. Grant’s wife, the American ceramicist Andrea Anderson, has thrown more than 950 pieces of pottery by hand for the hotel, a level of commitment to the breakfast table that seems almost unreasonable until one sees the results. The Brecon is adults-only and all-inclusive, organized around an open kitchen, with a sauna facing the mountains. While it’s not ski-in, ski-out, a free shuttle runs to the lifts, and a heated Art Deco pool awaits on your return.

Amenities: Restaurant, sauna, pool, shuttle

Editor’s tip: As an all-inclusive adults-only property, food, drinks, and spa access are included in the room rate.

At Kleine Scheidegg, beneath the Eiger, the Mönch, and the Jungfrau, the day ends when the last train leaves. The pass is accessible only by the Wengernalp railway, and once the final service has departed, the guests of the Bellevue des Alpes have the mountain largely to themselves.

The inn has stood here for generations: Christian Seiler bought it in 1840, and his descendants, the von Almens, still run it, with Andreas von Almen and his wife Silvia (a flutist), representing the fifth generation. The hotel was last extended in 1948, and little in the public rooms seems to have felt an urgent need for improvement since then. There is the grand piano, the old furnishings, and a bar dating to 1929, its swing door hung with photographs of the climbers and guides who used the hotel as a base camp for attempts on the Eiger’s north face. Guests would watch their progress through telescopes on the terrace, a rather more compelling form of entertainment than anything likely to appear on a hotel television. Clint Eastwood filmed The Eiger Sanction here in 1974, though the mountain itself has never needed Hollywood to establish its credentials. Skiing begins at the front door, and the setting is so imposing that the usual question of what else the hotel offers seems faintly beside the point.

Amenities: Restaurant, bar, terrace, ski-in, ski-out

Klosters acquired its Hollywood connections after the war, when American soldiers interned in Switzerland returned with their families and friends, and the film business followed. Greta Garbo, Gene Kelly, and Rex Harrison all appear in the guest book at the Chesa Grischuna, which earned the nickname “Hollywood on the Rocks”. The Guler family opened the hotel in 1938, and since 2022 it has been run by Zurich entrepreneurs Astrid von Stockar and Clemens Gregor. The entire building is a protected landmark, listed on Switzerland’s national register of historic places.

The thirteen rooms are furnished with antiques and local woodwork, and the old piano bar, whose walls are painted with winter scenes, is now a pasta bar—the natural gathering place after a day on the slopes. But the hotel’s best surprise lies below: a two-lane bowling alley painted by Alois Carigiet, the Swiss illustrator best known for A Bell for Ursli. Raclette is served in the adjoining tavern, which seems an entirely sensible way to recover from an evening of competitive bowling. One can understand why the Hollywood contingent came back: The Chesa Grischuna offers the sort of atmosphere that no amount of set dressing can quite manufacture, and has managed to preserve it without turning its history into a theme park.

Amenities: Restaurants, bar, bowling alley

Address: Bahnhofstrasse 12, 7250 Klosters-Serneus

Sils Maria has attracted writers and painters for well over a century. (Nietzsche among them: His summer house stands directly across the road from Chesa Marchetta.) The village lies between the lakes of Sils and Silvaplana, just fifteen minutes from St. Moritz, though it belongs to a rather different tradition of Engadin life—one more interested in contemplation than conspicuous consumption.

Chesa Marchetta occupies four connected farmhouse buildings dating to the sixteenth century. Artfarm, the hospitality company founded by Swiss gallerists Iwan and Manuela Wirth, whose other projects include Scotland’s Fife Arms, spent four years restoring the property before reopening it in January. The architect Luis Laplace retained the original sgraffito—the intricate scratched-plaster decoration that distinguishes the old houses of the valley—and furnished the thirteen rooms with traditional Engadin furniture, antiques, and work by local artists and artisans. Art, in other words, is not an accessory here so much as part of the building’s grammar.

Upstairs, the library and bar form the social heart of the house, a richly layered room where books, beautiful works of art and carefully chosen furnishings make for an atmosphere closer to a collector’s private residence than a conventional hotel lounge. It is the sort of place that invites you to linger over a drink, surrounded by objects with their own stories, without ever feeling overly designed. Downstairs, the restaurant draws on seasonal recipes, an Italian-Swiss mixture that makes good sense in a valley whose geography has never entirely respected national borders. Lake Sils is a fifteen-minute walk away, while Corvatsch is the nearest skiing.

Address: Via da Marias 88, 7514 Sils im Engadin/Segl

There are luxury hotels, and then there are institutions whose very existence has helped define luxury. Badrutt’s Palace, which opened in 1896, belongs rather emphatically to the latter category, having spent more than a century establishing the terms of alpine grandeur. Its unmistakable tower rises above the center of St. Moritz, overlooking the lake and the expensive little theater of Via Serlas, where the international winter set gathers each year to perform its familiar rituals of consumption.

Inside, the atmosphere is grand hotel in the fullest, least apologetic sense: chandeliers, imposing public rooms, formal service, and interiors that understand the importance of making an entrance. The original rooms remain reassuringly traditional, and the lake-facing ones are the ones worth asking for (Hitchcock, for his part, kept Suite 501). The Serlas Wing, opened in 2025, offers a contemporary counterpoint, its 25 rooms and suites by Antonio Citterio and Patricia Viel finished in local stone, oak, and Loro Piana Interiors wool. A three-minute walk from the property leads to Chesa Veglia, a 17th-century farmhouse housing several restaurants and bars, including beloved favorites, like Pizzeria Heuboden, the Carigiet Fondue Stübli and the Polo Bar, among others.

Back in the Palace, Matsuhisa occupies what was once Switzerland’s first indoor tennis hall, which is set to debut a reimagined design this winter by Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, while a new bar designed by Milanese designer Giuseppe Porcelli will welcome guests in Le Grand Hall. Up on Corviglia, Paradiso, the hotel’s mountain restaurant, trades chandeliers for panoramic views, Alpine fare, and a livelier après-ski scene. The Renaissance Bar is where the evening tends to end, preferably with a whisky, a cigar, and a seat by the fire. The spa’s glass-walled infinity pool looks straight out at the lake; even the business of doing very little ought to come with a view.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, bars, pool, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Founded by Johannes Badrutt in 1856, the Kulm helped establish St. Moritz as a winter resort. Set above the village with sweeping views across the Engadin, the hotel balances its sporting heritage with a distinctly contemporary appetite for reinvention. Many of its 150 rooms and suites have been refreshed by Pierre-Yves Rochon, while the restaurants range from Amaru, Claudia Canessa’s Peruvian-inspired restaurant dressed in contemporary whimsy by Luke Edward Hall, to Mauro Colagreco’s Kulm Country Club, housed in a neighboring building with its own ice rink. Sunny Bar, a St. Moritz institution in its own right, remains essential for a drink and a dose of local history.

The latest addition is the Alpine Sports Lounge & Boutique, designed by Foster + Partners for winter 2025. Clad in fragrant Swiss stone pine, it reimagines the conventional ski room with private fitting areas, specialist equipment, a ski concierge, and a pantry serving healthy snacks and energy shots. The idea is to get guests from suite to slope with rather less fuss, and considerably more style.

Amenities: Restaurants, bars, ice rink, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Few hotels have so thoroughly shaped the identity of the place they inhabit as Gstaad Palace has shaped that of Gstaad itself. Rising above the village like a white castle, it belongs to an older conception of luxury, when glamour required a little grandeur and there was an art to knowing exactly who was in the room (and that they may prefer not to announce themselves). Behind its turreted façade are ninety rooms and suites, five restaurants, a sprawling spa, indoor and outdoor pools, and the GreenGo, the legendary nightclub that has entertained generations of international society. Its corridors have absorbed the passing of royalty, financiers, and film stars.

One comes here, presumably, for the mountains, the service, and the fondue that’s served in a former wartime bunker. But one also comes for the sense of entering a world that has long since ceased to exist anywhere else—except, somehow, on this hill above Gstaad, where the old rituals of privilege continue to be performed with magnificent, almost theatrical conviction.

Amenities: Restaurants, spa, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Gstaad has always done luxury in a particular, old-money key, and The Alpina carries that tradition forward with a more contemporary hand. The 55 rooms are fitted with carved ceilings, timber walls and Swiss farmhouse cupboards, and even the leather straps once used to hang cowbells turn up as decoration. Meanwhile, above the main staircase is a hand-painted ceiling made in southern Europe around 1780 and painstakingly restored. New executive chef Francesco De Bartolomeis oversees the hotel’s entire food offering, so dinner can be Japanese at Megu or Bernese at the Swiss Stübli, with a cellar of 1,700-plus labels behind either. It isn’t ski-in, ski-out, but a shuttle runs to the lifts and the hotel sorts passes and rentals. The Six Senses Spa is vast, and its menu runs from Tibetan healing to bio-hacking therapies, such as their hyperbaric oxygen chamber.

Amenities: Restaurants, spa, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Suvretta House occupies a rather different corner of the St. Moritz universe. Opened in 1912, it sits away from the village center, surrounded by mountain scenery and woodland, in a position that feels deliberately removed from the main procession of boutiques, champagne bars, and other seasonal distractions. Its fairytale exterior and grand interiors are unapologetically old-world, retaining the grandeur and traditions of the great Alpine hotels, but with a more secluded, sporting character. This is a hotel for people who regard a ski holiday as something that ought to involve actual skiing: It has direct ski-in/ski-out access to the Corviglia slopes, its own ski facilities, and a long-standing connection to the mountain that sets it apart from properties in the village.

For lunch on the slopes, there’s Trutz, near the top of the Suvretta lift, while Chasellas, down at the base, is the place to stop for a hot chocolate after skiing. Back at the hotel, the Grand Restaurant offers an altogether more formal expression of Alpine luxury, with elaborate interiors, traditional service and a culinary repertoire that combines French influences with international touches. Among its most famous dishes is spaghetti with caviar, a luxurious yet understated signature that reflects the Grand Restaurant’s timeless elegance. Afternoon tea and a swim in the pool within the hotel’s expansive, freshly renovated spa complete the experience. Suvretta’s particular appeal lies in this combination of grandeur, sporting heritage, and seclusion… with a hotel shuttle to bring you into town in a matter of minutes whenever you’re ready to rejoin the scene.

Amenities: Spa, restaurants, pool, ski-in, ski-out, shuttle, on-site ski rental

Address: Via Chasellas 1, 7500 St. Moritz

#6610. 12 Todd Snyder Gifts That Even Menswear Snobs Will Appreciate

There’s a certain kind of guy who’s impossible to shop for. You know the one: he’s had the same pair of resoled boots since 2015, can tell you exactly why his Oxford shirt is better than yours, and has strong opinions about how wide a pant leg should be. Pleasing him might seem hopeless, but there’s a cheat code, and it’s called Todd Snyder. The brand has spent more than a decade quietly perfecting the American wardrobe: the sweaters, cords and jackets that look like they’ve been in his closet forever, only better.

Consider this your shortcut. I went shopping the way I always do and pulled the Todd Snyder gifts I’d be thrilled to unwrap. All that’s left for you to do is pick one and maybe hide the receipt, since he won’t be needing it. Fair warning: there’s a good chance you’ll end up buying something for yourself, too. ‘Tis the season.

A barn jacket gets an upgrade. Flocked denim gives it a velvety, suede-like surface, and the leather collar adds a nice bit of contrast. It’s rugged enough for a weekend upstate and polished enough for a swanky dinner in the city.

Cords are back in a big way, and it’s not just vintage obsessives wearing them: they’ve become the go-to cold-weather pant for guys who want something softer than denim. This straight leg camel pair is an easy way to add some warmth and texture to his wardrobe. He’ll wear them just like his favorite 501’s.

Every guy needs one great flannel, and this blue-and-cream plaid is it. It’s soft enough to wear on its own and sturdy enough to layer as a light jacket on milder days.

A cashmere sweater is the gift that never misses, and this rich red version is perfect for the holidays without screaming “Christmas sweater.” It’s the kind of thing he’ll pull on every December for years.

Colorful flecks of Donegal yarn take a simple black beanie somewhere much more interesting. It’s cashmere too, so he’ll actually want to wear it instead of stashing it away in a coat pocket in case of emergency.

Supple leather on the outside and cashmere on the inside: this is a cold-weather essential done right. It’s a grown-up upgrade over the gloves he’s been losing every winter since college.

An olive wool bomber with a plush shearling collar hits the sweet spot between a flight jacket and a proper winter coat. It works with everything from cords to tailored trousers. Bonus points since it will look better every season after some wear and tear..

For the guy who lives in dark denim, black cords are a smart switch. They’re just as versatile, much cozier, and dress up easier than you’d think.

Brushed cotton turns the camp collar into a fall shirt. The muted plaid and relaxed fit make it a great layering piece over a tee, or something to wear buttoned up on its own when the heat’s cranked indoors.

The waffle knit gives this navy sweater a depth and texture that a flat knit can’t match. It’s understated in the best way: the kind of piece that gets compliments without trying too hard.

Joshua Ellis has been weaving cloth in Yorkshire since the 18th century, and it shows. This bold red tartan is the coat accessory that does the most work, brightening up even the gloomiest January commute.

Pleats, a roomy leg and a flecked silk-Donegal fabric from Italy make this the dress pant for guys who don’t like dress pants. It’s sharp enough for the office party and relaxed enough to wear with a sweater the next morning.

#6609. Stylist and Creative Director Akari Endo-Gaut’s Guide to Tokyo

Perhaps no city juggles the past and the future as nimbly as Tokyo. Sleek skyscrapers meet centuries-old shrines; a rich culinary tradition blends with contemporary innovation (it’s no accident that this is the city with the most Michelin starred-restaurants in the world). The fashion, of course, exists in a similar dichotomy, expertly blending traditional techniques with the avant-garde. There’s never a wrong time to visit the Japanese capital—but in winter, when ski resorts a quick day trip away are in full swing and New Year’s celebrations are on the horizon, it feels particularly special. All you have to do is narrow down your itinerary.

In fact, there’s so much to discover that you could spend an entire trip dedicated to shopping alone—according to Akari Endo-Gaut, a Japan-born, New York-based stylist and creative director who studied in Tokyo, it may be worth bringing a second suitcase just for souvenirs. From the vintage shops to put on your radar to the best place to stop for a glass of natural wine, here’s a glimpse at Endo-Gaut’s Tokyo little black book.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Since I was student in Tokyo, one of my favorite areas to hang around was Minami-Aoyama. We used to have amazing Corso Como store there; now, the Comme des Garçons store, the Issey Miyake Pleats Please shop, and the Auralee store there are still where you can go to find a special piece.

For vintage gems: There are so many good vintage shops in Tokyo, and it goes deep. BerBer Jin is always my first stop, and I also check luxury resale shops like Komehyo.

For unique souvenirs: You can find the best curated products, from ceramic bowls to German knives, at Arts and Science. And beautifully wrapped sweets at Higashiya are the best gifts.

For a worthwhile investment piece: Wako Arts and Culture is a new space conceived by artist Hiroshi Sugimoto in the basement of a prestigious department store in Ginza. It’s all specially curated, a great spot to find a special piece from fashion to Japanese craft.

For the magpie: My very talented friend Charlotte Chesnais from Paris recently opened a shop in Tokyo; it’s a must-visit. Or, if you’re looking for best-condition vintage watches, you can go to ECW Shoto.

For your next great read: Japan has a big book culture—go to Komiyama bookstore for vintage books, or spend a full weekend browsing at Tsutaya Daikanyama or SKAC.

For stylish home goods: You can find traditional but beautiful kitchen goods at Kiya and, of course, at Muji. Or, spend a fun day exploring all the kitchen goods stores in the Kappabashi area, which is a shopping street dedicated to restaurant owners.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Hakujitsu houses a beautiful collection of ceramics in an old dentist building. My secret favorite is Yanaka Matsunoya—it has the best baskets and tote bags.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Japanese-Chinese food or yakiniku, so I go to Chugoku Hanten with local friends or to Jojoen with my sister. If I have foreign guests, they usually have fun dining experience at Narukiyo.

For a bakery treat: Sawamura is our best local bakery cafe in Hiroo. After a soba lunch at Kanda, stop by Omiya Western Sweets Shop for the cutest pastry; for traditional Japanese sweets at an upscale, architecturally beautiful spot, go to Toraya Akasaka.

For the art-lover: Taka Ishii and Tomio Koyama are the best fine arts galleries in Tokyo. I like the artists from Kosaku Kanechika too, and at Licht gallery, you can see the best design pieces.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: For the architecture lover, a drink at Imperial Bar, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, is a must. When I’m hanging out with local friends, I’d go for a natural wine at Le Cabaret or Tabac.

For your packing list: Honestly, you don’t need anything, since you go to Tokyo to buy the best of all items! Bring flat shoes for walking, and an extra suitcase for shopping. An eye mask and melatonin for the 13-hour time difference will come in handy, as will a handkerchief; it’s part of local etiquette to carry one. And I always like to bring a running outfit for the famous Imperial Palace run.

#6607. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6606. The Governors Awards Marked the Official Start of the 'You Can See Everything' Oscars Campaign

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

Start your engines: the 2027 Oscars race is officially underway. Awards Season always starts in earnest with the Governors Awards, a ceremony held in a smaller ballroom in the same Dolby Theater complex where the main event will take place early next spring. It’s where they give out honorary Academy Awards (and the esteemed Irving Thalberg Award) to the legends who, woefully, have yet have won a competitive Oscar—last year’s marquee honoree was Tom Cruise, this year’s were Glenn Close and Ridley Scott. But it’s also where Best Picture and the other awards narratives we will discuss endlessly for the next four months really begin to take shape.

Dune 3, Artificial, and Misty Green all had big presences in the room, which, duh. (Tim and Kylie in the cut, mostly sitting and not mingling, but it was interesting that he showed up this year but not last for the big Marty Supreme push.) But there were a few other films represented whose presence made their campaign intentions clear. Mahershala Ali presented the first award of the night to Floyd Norman (a 90-year-old trailblazing cartoonist who worked with Walt Disney and later Pete Docter) but the Your Mother 3x squad was deep, from director Bassam Tariq to John Cho. Jesse Eisenberg, Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore put on for A24’s The Debut, Eisenberg's second directorial effort. (Watching Jesse and Andrew Garfield reconnect made for a beautiful Social Network reunion.) And Curry Barker and Inde Navarette being there would certainly imply a real push for Obsession. The duo with the most motion in the room, though, was unquestionably Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The only time they didn’t seem like the big dogs that everyone was gassed to chat with was when they were talking to King Big Dog himself, Christopher Nolan, front and center receiving will-wishers at The Odyssey table. Nolan and Fielder is a crossover that needs to be cemented on wax, a drum I will continue to beat. But it was cool to see Zendaya talking intently with Oppenheim; her collaborator curation has been pretty elite—imagine her in whatever Oppenheim chooses to follow Primetime with?

When I asked Fielder about embarking on the campaign trail and how far the doc can actually go, he sighed and said “one day at a time,” in that Fielder monotone where you can’t quite tell if he’s being earnest or not. But he laughed off the idea of being too invested in any nominations either way.

But most importantly: the Governors Awards is just a really fun room in which to be an interloper or fly on the wall. I spotted Shawn Levy and my brain immediately started spamming the word “sublime.” Daniel Kaluuya started cracking up at the mention of his great airport interview with Tyriq Withers. Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Ed Norton joined ranks for a brief Invite huddle. Everywhere I turned, there was either a person so famous or certified that it startled me to see them walk by (like Zendaya breezing in right as the show started, or turning around to find myself face-to-face with personal favorite Carla Gugino. (Karen Sisco mentioned!) Unlike some stuffier award ceremonies, the Governors Awards is kind of like the cocktail hour before the big sit-down dinner in March.

Ambling around the room with a stiff glass of Johnnie Walker in hand—“Did you just get carded”? an exec asked me incredulously; the bartender replied that he thought I was “like, 14"—I briefly caught up with David Corenswet, who, true to form, was unfazed by the forces beyond his control as ever. When I said “weird week huh?” he didn’t even realize I was referring to James Gunn’s DC exit, then laughed when it dawned on him and said “above my pay-grade” with a genuine shrug. We should all be so blissfully unbothered.

Later, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II told me he was excited for this week’s Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth red carpet premiere, noting that this film will be the first time he only read his scenes for a project and no other part of the story. Without wanting to give too much away, Yahya said Tarantino’s script is structured in a way where he could comfortably read his parts and get enough of the gist to stay in the dark about the rest, because the only thing better than starring in a new Tarantino joint is getting to still experience it like a fan.

Other notable sightings, interactions, and crossovers: Travis Scott doubled down on what he told me at our Men of the Year party: he wants that golden statue for his original Odyssey song, and he’s willing to play the campaign game for it, dutifully sitting through the whole night (and jetting off immediately after the ceremony ended to go catch Future’s 10 pm set at Camp Flog Gnaw up at Dodger Stadium.) Speaking of Odyssey collaborators, James Blake was also in attendance—I watched him meet H.E.R. and talk about potentially collaborating. Tom Cruise was the belle of the ball at last year’s ceremony but played it super lowkey this year, to the point where I didn’t actually realize he was there until I saw him sneak out of a secret side exit after briefly talking with Tessa Thompson. Digger’s divisive reviews and reactions have evidently not knocked Tom off of his Best Actor pivot.

As for the actual awards, after Floyd, John Malkovich charmed the room with a great toast to Glenn Close, and King Storyteller Matt Damon regaled everyone with a great impression of triple-OG crank Ridley Scott from their time together on The Martian. (Matt was hesitant to do another movie about a loner astronaut right after Interstellar, to which Ridley apparently replied “No one gives a shit.”) Both tributes and subsequent speeches were expectedly emotional; Damon pointedly said that "it’s about time we see Ridley Scott with an Oscar in his hand,” but Ridley’s remarks were all about how much the late great Tony Scott would’ve deserved one too, leading to misty eyes and standing ovations. Close addressed going 0 for 8 but said the work is the real reward as her daughter tearfully watched on. But there were great moments of levity, too, like Todd Haynes presenting Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with an award by revealing that he and Christine both slept with the same guy back in college.

Either way, a narrative of being long overdue seems to be emerging. An Awards Season where the Tom Cruises and Glenn Closes of the game finally get theirs, while upsets like You Can See Everything shake the table. What more could you ask for?

#6605. The Fearless Sensitivity of ‘Mouse’ and ‘Clarissa’ Star Sophie Okonedo

Sophie Okonedo is one of those performers whose very presence can make a scene feel more alive. The Tony Award-winning British actress projects both warmth and watchfulness, moving swiftly from humor to hurt, or authority to vulnerability, without announcing the shift. Even in a supporting role, she has a way of making you lean in.

This winter, she leads two independent features opening theatrically after an international festival run: Clarissa, by brothers Chuko and Arie Esiri, and Mouse, by the husband-and-wife team of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. Though shot nearly a year apart, the two films are arriving within weeks of each other—a quirk of the release calendar that makes for an unusually timely double feature.

Mouse, out now, is a coming-of-age story set in 2002 Arkansas, in which the teenage Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer) develops a complicated relationship with her best friend’s mother (Okonedo) after an unexpected tragedy. Meanwhile, Clarissa—in limited theaters December 18—transposes Virginia Woolf’s novel Mrs. Dalloway to contemporary Nigeria, a project that brought Okonedo to a country she hadn’t visited in two decades. (Her late father, whom she was mostly estranged from, moved back to his home country when she was young.)

Filming in Lagos proved consequential in ways that extended well beyond the work itself. “The journey I had in Lagos was so immense, personally and professionally, that I remember thinking on the wrap day that even if nothing else happens with this film, I’ve already gotten everything I wanted,” she tells me.

Both films were made on tiny budgets, and, as Okonedo points out, a conversation about one inevitably opens up a conversation about the other. So, we talked about both.

Vogue: Let’s start with Mouse. How did it come to you? What was it about your character Helen, or about directors Kelly and Alex, that made you say yes?

Sophie Okonedo: I didn’t read anything about them. I read the script completely cold. By the time I got to the end, I rang my agent and said, “I’m absolutely doing this. I don’t know who’s directing, I don’t know what’s happening with the film, but I’m doing it.” So he sent me their last film, Ghostlight. It’s such a brilliant film and it was made for pennies. These are two really interesting filmmakers who are talking about America in a way I haven’t seen—very quietly. There are no explosions, no big movie stars, and it’s deeply significant. Kelly’s writing is subtle and real. But films like this can slip by without anyone noticing. I have to galvanize everyone and get them behind it, because I think it’s so good.

Helen ends up mothering her daughter’s friend, Minnie, in a way that’s unnerving at times, as if she’s grieving and replacing her at the same time.

It’s totally inappropriate at times. She even says it at one point: “Oh my God, I’m the adult here.” She uses Minnie to ease her own grief, then backtracks, then moves forward again. It’s a messy situation, but there’s hope in it. The film is funny, too. Kelly has that gift for finding levity in dark situations. But they never get you to play the comedy. You play the seriousness of it all and it’s funny as it goes along.

I realized after watching the film that the woman playing Katherine’s mother is her real-life mother. What was that dynamic like on set?

She wasn’t even meant to play the part at first. Tara [Kupferer], her mother, is a theater actress. She runs a theater company in Chicago and was there as Katherine’s guardian. They’d cast a great local actor, but on the first day we realized it wasn’t right. By the second day, Tara stepped in. Everything was so homegrown. My baby in the film is actually Kelly and Alex’s baby. They removed all the blockers you normally have as an actor on a film, where you spend three hours in hair and makeup. Sometimes you need those things, but this film didn’t. You just rock up and start filming. It was very seamless.

Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Sophie Okonedo in Mouse.

You shot on location in North Little Rock. Had you been to Arkansas before?

Never. I got there a little early to check it out because I was playing an outsider, but an outsider who’d lived there for 15 years, so I had to know the place and feel familiar with it. All the locations came from [O’Sullivan’s] childhood; you could ask her, “What happened here?” and she’d tell you. A lot of people with small parts in the film knew Kelly from high school and were now playing mothers. The dance we see at the memorial was one Kelly actually performed herself. We even brought back the dance teacher who taught her so she could teach it to the two girls in the film.

Does playing an outsider give you something to work with? You didn’t do the method thing, keeping yourself apart from everyone, right?

No. I totally get that some people do, but I’m too shy to stay in character! I feel too silly. What I do is think very deeply about every single word I say in the script before I arrive. Because I’m theater-trained, the script is my bible. All answers will be there. I spend a long time thinking about everything I say and everything everyone else says, and I go through it many, many times. An internal world builds up inside me. I can’t really explain how it happens. When I get to set, I forget any notes or journals I’ve made. I drop it all, empty myself, and see what happens. I feel buoyant and flexible, not stuck in any particular way.

Mouse is so specific about 2002, down to the Michelle Branch music cues. I was a bit younger than the characters then, but it all felt right. What did setting it in that moment bring to the story?

I’m older, but Kelly was that age in 2002, so she had all the references. She knew exactly what she was listening to, what she was thinking and feeling. The main difference is there were no cell phones back then. If you wanted information, it had to come to you through someone taking action. The jogger has to tell Minnie something, then she has to run to the house to see if it’s really happened, then she has to look for a phone book. Now it would just be someone posting “RIP Callie” on Instagram. It’s so much more interesting to film people taking an action than all these constant shots of phones and texts, which I see in movies all the time now. It’s so boring.

In Mouse, Helen and Minnie come from very different backgrounds. Class is also woven into Clarissa, where you play the titular role. Was that a connection you were conscious of while working on the two films?

Class is massive in Britain. We live and breathe it. It runs through every vein of everyone’s body here, probably more than anything else, so I’m very aware of it. But there’s another weird parallel between the films: Mouse is directed by a couple and one of them is the writer. Clarissa is directed by two brothers and one of them is the writer. With both, I had an instant, visceral response. I didn’t need to think about the whys and wherefores. It was just yes, yes, yes. With a lot of other work, I have to get myself into the right position or work it out. What’s also amazing is that the scripts for Clarissa and Mouse barely changed between that first draft and the start of filming—the same was true of Janet Planet. These are filmmakers who have thought deeply about what they’re writing. There weren’t a million drafts or endless revisions; all three films were already in a remarkably evolved state from the start. Even though Mouse looks improvised in places, I’m sticking to the script.

But parts of Mouse were improvised, right? I’m thinking of the scene where Helen attends a grief group.

It was a real grief group. I knew the man handing me coffee at the beginning was an actor, though by coincidence he was also in a grief group. I was just outside the room; they put two cameras in there and someone called action. I walked in, and during the scene it slowly dawned on me—someone had forgotten to tell me these weren’t actors!

The scene is short, but that take lasted an hour and 10 minutes—the exact length of the group. If it were scripted, I probably would have talked and broken down. But I couldn’t speak; their stories were so extraordinary. I was still talking to them afterward, thinking the cameras had stopped, when I realized they were still filming. Alex will do that. You don’t even know. There’s no “cut.”

Both films are concerned with motherhood, though in very different ways. In Mouse, there’s an absent daughter; in Clarissa, she keeps her living daughter at arm’s length. Did these characters speak to each other in any way?

It’s a good question, because I find that when I do a part, it usually feeds into the next one. The next role I played after Clarissa was Natalya in Turgenev’s A Month in the Country, in London. She’s a woman of a certain age looking back, wondering whether she made the right choices, and she has a very separate relationship with her son. I was thinking that a lot of Clarissa was in her.

I read that Arie and Chuko drew on their own mother in shaping the film, and that you got to spend time with her. How did that influence your performance?

When they cast me, I wondered if I could do this. I told them I didn’t recognize the Lagos in the script and that I had such a fractured relationship with the country. They said, “If nothing else, we’ll bridge that for you.” That meant a lot. Before filming, Chuko invited me to stay with him and his mother. I ended up staying the whole shoot and got very close to her. I used a lot of her, more than she realizes perhaps. Like Clarissa, she employs staff [in her home] and I observed how she interacted with them. I didn’t want to turn her into a caricature out of Downton Abbey. You can just be real with them, the way she was.

You also just don’t see stories like this coming out of Africa, and I say that broadly. The subject matter is usually very narrow: Africa is depicted as war-torn, impoverished. Here was a film about people. There’s a backdrop of war and social and economic circumstances, but that isn’t the main thrust. I long to see films where we as Africans, as Nigerians, get every part of ourselves represented, just as our white Western counterparts get films about everything. It’s the same with queer films and Black films: they shouldn’t only be about being queer or Black. That shouldn’t have to be the whole story.

And on top of that, Clarissa is character-driven and not plot-driven.

The thought of going to Lagos and making an arthouse film on 35mm was incredible. It’s an impossible book to film. People have tried many times, and mostly it doesn’t work. I was taking a punt. I just wanted to be part of it. I hardly say anything, but say a million words with my face.

What is it like to project that kind of interiority? It’s sort of a paradox: Clarissa is deep in thought but she also doesn't let you in much.

She’s hard to read, but you have to make her really easy to read for the camera. She’s protective, but you have to let the camera in. I didn’t think about it that deeply. I just have that sort of face. I’m really sensitive, hypersensitive, which is so difficult in my normal life, but it’s great for acting. My grandmother used to say, “Your face changes like the wind.” Everything shows. Chuko or Arie would only have to whisper the slightest thing in my ear, and it would show.

People always say to watch an actor’s eyes, but I noticed so much happens in the lower half of your face. It holds everything.

That’s why I could never do any of that stuff to my face. I’d be too frightened! I know I only have to think the glimmer of a thought and it’ll show. I don’t know what happens to my face, because I don’t really watch myself, but doing something that would stop that would be the end of my career.

The story famously centers on your character throwing a party. Are you more of a host or a guest?

I’m quite a good host, actually. I don’t do it often because I go overboard and it’s exhausting. I love cooking and making lovely things. I used to spend the whole time panicking in the kitchen, but I’ve learned it doesn’t really matter what you serve. It’s about how you engage with guests. They just want you to be part of the party.

Did you watch any of the other adaptations of Mrs. Dalloway to prepare for Clarissa?

I watched about three minutes of one with Vanessa Redgrave and realized we’re not doing this type of film, so I didn’t carry on. Chuko and Arie would have watched everything, though. They're complete cinephiles.

Did they give you suggestions on films to watch to prepare then?

They probably did, but I forgot because my brain is a sieve. They gave up on me. They’d mention really famous films and I’d say I hadn’t seen them. I don’t know what I do with my time. I don’t fill it wisely. I just seem to mess around most of the day, and then it’s gone!

It sounds like you’re living your own stories instead of watching other people’s on screen.

You’re putting it nicely. As my husband says, I spend a lot of time daydreaming. I’ve got a really nice view. [She turns her laptop to the window to show me the view.] I spend a lot of time just looking out at the trees with my dog.

After this double-header year, what are you looking for next?

Because I’m getting older, I don’t see an eternity stretching out in front of me anymore, and I find myself asking how I want to spend my time. I’ve decided that my heart is really in independent films and theater, so I’m going to wait until the right thing comes along. You might find me still unemployed a year from now. Nothing has come up yet that’s been worth getting on a plane for.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6604. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6603. Andy Baraghani's Ditto Café Is His Most Personal Project Yet

Andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying. Stagnancy, he’s quick to clarify, is different from stillness. Stagnancy is like a fetid pond; stillness is meditative. Baraghani seems to be at risk of neither.

It is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen. He is about to make me scones—salty-sweet ones with dates and lemon zest, an offering under development for his forthcoming café Ditto. But first, we’ll need to pop out for cream.

Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he says.

He lives just a few blocks from the Union Square Greenmarket, where niche pepper varieties are currently splayed in colorful fractals across folding tables. We have just completed a ground floor tour of the apartment that the chef-cum-writer-cum-chef shares with his husband, Keith Pollock. Now he moves across the kitchen and pauses at the Crittall-style window. It gives me 30 seconds to take inventory of his countertop alliums.

These details feel important. Baraghani has become a sort of standard-bearer for exquisite seasonal produce and the exquisite life one can lead preparing such stuff. I clock a couple of shallots, which sit in a Swid Powell bowl beside five heirloom tomatoes. It occurs to me that even onions are more beautiful in Baraghani’s universe.

“Oh,” he says casually, following my gaze. “Torpedo shallots.” As if all of our countertops look like this.

In the decade or so since he became a household name for a certain set of a certain era (food-obsessed aesthetes who love an acidic drizzle and a hard, salty cheese), as a video star for a certain magazine—okay, this one—his fandom has only continued to explode.

His debut cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be, was a New York Times bestseller and the recipient of a James Beard Award. He has more than 370,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok. He’s been called “the Internet boyfriend of our dreams.” Vogue covered his wedding. The New York Times published his ideal Thanksgiving menu. In the last 24 hours alone, Baraghani has been busy beating out creative director Terrence O’Connor for a Best Body prize at the podcast How Long Gone’s inaugural “Goneies” Award Show, (Baraghani was asked to remove his blazer to reveal a formfitting Dario Vitale–era Versace pink tank top) before running into David Tanis while shopping for groceries.

When Baraghani announced he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. Still, he says, few have pushed him on the true meaning of the name Ditto. Perhaps they were too busy trying to keep up.

Baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. I inquire about his cortisol levels as he juggles opening Ditto a few blocks away, the second cookbook he has just shot in this apartment, and now the remodel below us.

Baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”

He has spent the last 10 years peppering his recipes with caveats. “I know that my food may be a touch too lemony for some,” he writes in The Cook You Want To Be. “And that I use what has been called a ridiculous amount of herbs.”

His background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. The piece ended with an admission: “So as nice as it would be for this story to end with that Iran feature or getting my dream job at Bon Appétit, the truth is that I’m still trying to figure things out. It’s not always steady progress.”

Since I had a baby six weeks ago, I have been walking around floored that the adults in my life could have ever been children, but with Andy, I don’t have to work too hard to picture it. He has a particularly cheerful sense of wonder. When I ask about it, he says it comes from his upbringing. His parents were political activists. Andy’s mother worked as an aesthetician (yes, he established his famous skin-care routine early). He grew up surrounded by a diverse community of immigrants who would invite his family to their celebrations and into their homes, where a young Baraghani got to taste dishes from far-flung places. After he landed in New York, he would take respite in stints abroad, traveling from hostel to hostel so he could eat his way across Vietnam, Lebanon, and Turkey.

Now, though, Baraghani says he is done footnoting his vision. In the intervening years since that essay, Baraghani has written and cooked and tasted at warp speed. He was bound to self-actualize in the same timeframe it took the rest of us to figure out how to style barrel-leg pants. Or perhaps it’s the reality of having to reckon with what he can’t change: In 2024, after a battle with small-cell lung cancer, his beloved father passed away. Baraghani tells me that before it was stagnancy, his greatest fear was losing a parent. He has since learned that loss isn’t something to solve, but a tremendous void one must learn to live with.

“There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see [at Ditto,]” he says. The dishes will weave together all of the threads of Baraghani-ism: seasonal vegetables prepared deftly with Persian flourishes, blending tart and sour and aromatic with a firm point-of-view. If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.)

Literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in New York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with plans for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

The goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was important for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the plan is breakfast and lunch.

Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

The sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.)

Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

As we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he says simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

Later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

And for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.
