Available sizes: 10", 12", 14"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime

About stainless steel: Stainless-steel cookware is a staple in home and professional kitchens because of its versatility, durability, and low maintenance needs. Use it on the stovetop, in the oven, or with metal tools—unlike shorter-lived ceramic pans, a stainless-steel skillet can serve you well for a lifetime. And here’s the thing: With the proper technique, stainless steel can release almost as easily as ceramic nonstick. The key in guaranteeing your food slides right off instead of becoming a stuck-on mess is using sufficient fat and heat. Make sure to wait until your oil is shimmering before adding whatever you’re cooking, give it enough time in the pan to let the maillard reaction do its thing, and you should have no issues with stickage.

Our top pick: We’ve tested many types of stainless-steel cookware throughout the years here at BA, and one brand has repeatedly stood out time and time again for its consistently well-made, durable, high-performing products. That brand is All-Clad.

In our testing of stainless-steel frying pans and sauté pans, product testers and Test Kitchen editors alike lauded All-Clad’s D3 Everyday line as the best mix of value and performance for home cooks. The “3” refers to these pans’ 3-ply construction, which features an aluminum core sandwiched between two layers of stainless-steel cladding. That aluminum allows the pan to conduct heat quickly and evenly, and it makes the pan more lightweight than solid stainless-steel cookware. In our testing, we found that those promises held true, and that the D3 pans were easy to clean (just hand-wash with a little soapy water, plus some Bar Keepers Friend if you need a hand getting any remaining bits off) and have continued to perform well over the many years we’ve been using them.

About cast iron: If you’re willing to put just a bit of work into caring for your cookware, a cast-iron skillet will easily fill the nonstick pan-size hole in your kitchen. Cast-iron cookware will never quite reach the level of nonstick that a Teflon-coated piece offers, but in our testing, we’ve found that a properly seasoned cast-iron pan is on par with ceramic nonstick—plus it only gets more slick over time as you continue to use it.

Our top pick: After testing more than 20 cast-iron skillets over several years, our current top pick is the Lancaster No. 8 because it’s lightweight, it has a smooth pre-seasoned surface that’s nice and slick right out of the box, and it provides even heat distribution. The one downside is that it’s quite pricey compared to something like Lodge’s iconic cast iron, which we recommend as a great budget alternative. The Lodge is probably the pan most people think of when they hear “cast-iron skillet,” and at around $20, depending on where and when you buy it, it’s one of the best values in the cookware world—particularly because you can keep it forever rather than replacing it every few years. In our testing, it performed just as well as many more expensive pans.

About enameled cast iron: You may have also heard of enameled cast iron, which is frequently seen in products like our favorite Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens. Many people expect enameled cast-iron pots and pans to be nonstick because the ones with light-colored interiors sort of resemble the kinds of ceramic nonstick coatings we wrote about above, but in reality, that’s not the case. That doesn’t mean you can’t cook food in these things without it sticking, but you’ll need to use sufficient fat and heat to make that happen, as you do with a stainless-steel pan. The benefit of enameled cast iron is that it provides superior heat retention and distribution, and protects the cast-iron core from rust and acidity. It's become one of my favorite types of cookware to use at home over the past few years.

Our top pick: The Staub Round Cocotte is my personal top pick when it comes to Dutch ovens, and tied with the Le Creuset in our official product testing. I prefer the Staub’s dark textured enamel interior, which is less prone to showing discoloration. In addition to the round cocotte, I also own the braiser and a deep skillet, both of which I find myself pulling out constantly.

Read more about our favorite Dutch ovens.

Available sizes: 8", 10.25", 11", 12.5"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime

About carbon steel: Carbon steel is sort of the Goldilocks cookware because it affords you the nonstick qualities and lightweight feel of a coated nonstick pan and the durability of a cast-iron or stainless-steel skillet. The one caveat is that in order to achieve those nonstick qualities, you’ll need to spend some time properly seasoning your new pan, just as you would with cast iron. But with a bit of work at the outset and occasional maintenance, you’ll be rewarded with an heirloom-worthy piece of cookware that has a well-earned nonstick patina.

Our top pick: De Buyer is one of those famed, old European cookware brands that lots of American home cooks may not be that familiar with. Its “blue” frying pan comes pre-seasoned and will just get better and better as the seasoning improves. As senior writer Wilder Davies notes, you can take specific steps to season it—use a thin layer of oil (as thin as you can possibly get) and put it in a hot oven for an hour—but you can also just keep cooking with it and that seasoning will develop on its own. Another nice feature of this pan in particular, and one that has nothing to do with its seasoning, is its welded-on handle. That means there are no rivets to clean around when you’re done.

Read more about our favorite carbon steel pans.

What types of kitchen gear is PTFE found in?

A skillet may be the first thing you think of when you think of nonstick cookware, but PTFE coatings show up in a host of other items in the kitchen and beyond. On top of skillets, pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, you'll also find PTFE in rice cookers, waffle irons, baking sheets, and grill baskets.

You may recognize ceramic nonstick as the material of choice of many of the aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-viral cookware companies that started popping up in the late 2010s (I’m looking at you, Our Place and Caraway). Ceramic nonstick pans are made without any PFAS. Instead, a gel made from silica is applied and then dried onto the cookware’s metal body to create a nonstick surface.

Sounds great, right? Well, there are a few caveats, the main one being that ceramic nonstick coatings are not built to last. That means you’ll want to be sure to avoid using metal utensils when cooking with them, opting instead for wood or silicone. You’ll also want to avoid exposing them to extremely high temperatures: Even though ceramic cookware is technically more heat tolerant than cookware made with PTFE, high heat will wear down the pan’s ceramic coating. Many manufacturers claim their pans are oven-safe up to certain (often high) temperatures, but we’d recommend using one of our other recommendations above for any stove-to-oven cooking, as those trips to the oven will only further degrade that ceramic coating over time. Similarly, despite any of being dishwasher-safe, hand-washing your pans will prolong their lifespans.

Even if you treat your ceramic nonstick cookware with the utmost care and attention, you still shouldn’t expect it to last you more than one to three years before it starts to lose its nonstick properties. That’s why the best nontoxic nonstick cookware is not necessarily a coated piece of PFOA- or PFAS-free gear—in fact, we’d argue the best nontoxic “nonstick” pans money can buy are made of cast iron, or carbon steel. While these materials are not actually manufactured or marketed as nonstick, each has nonstick properties that can be achieved with proper use and care. .

The bottom line here is that no one needs a coated pan in their life. There is no recipe on this website (or in this world) that requires you to use one, and we tend to think you’re better off investing some time in learning to cook with a more durable type of cookware than spending you money on a full nonstick cookware set. That said, we’re recommending a range of cookware options here for those who are looking for alternatives to traditional PTFE-base nonstick, including a ceramic option for people who aren’t quite ready to kiss coated nonstick goodbye.

#6562. How Celine’s Michael Rider Quietly Seized Fashion’s Attention

You can tell a lot about a designer by the scene backstage after a show. Usually, it’s sweaty, manic, crammed with hangers-on—the fashion equivalent of an airport lounge during a blizzard. But on the unseasonably warm October day of Michael Rider’s most recent Paris runway show, the space was alive with Champagne toasts and bubbly conversation.

The co-ed summer 2027 runway was a blowout party hosted by Rider with models channeling twitchy new-wave dancers, preppy ’80s croquet players, and the heroic DIY divas from Paris Is Burning. Rider showed new tailoring shapes for men, specifically loose, floppy blazers and slim cigarette-leg pants, cropped confidently above the ankle. A showstopping look of gleaming pink separates somehow avoided silliness. Rider’s signature styling took the edge off. A silver shimmering suit was mildly de-glammed by a jacket tied around the waist. A jaunty black hat topped off an outfit with a white long-sleeve shirt and shorts. Improbably, these wild ideas felt coherent—a hard-won sleight of hand.

In the garden of the National Archives Museum, friends of Rider like Hannah Einbinder, Tracee Ellis Ross, and Dan Levy milled around waiting for the designer to finish telling critics about his “intuitive” approach to fashion. Like something out of Lewis Carroll, a spread was unfurled on a long outdoor table. Waiters poured Champagne into a tower of coupes; editors licked homemade popsicles and bit into crunchy sandwiches of jambon-beurre. No one seemed like they had anywhere to be. This was the place to be.

In less than two years, Rider has cleaned the slate following Hedi Slimane’s shrunken, skinny rock era at Celine. He’s brought more accessible, artfully styled fashion to the stores. He’s delivered at least two hit shoes: the dirty white jazz lace-up, and, this past September, an immediately sold-out collaboration with Reebok that reissued the 1982 Freestyle Lo sneaker in decadent leather, in shades from oxblood to buttery yellow.

In the process, his Celine has become a favorite among fashion-minded men. Ebon Moss-Bachrach, the tall Girls and The Bear actor, told me backstage that Rider’s menswear feels “masculine without any kind of footnote.” Youngjae, from the K-pop band TWS, explained the allure of Rider’s vision. “The Celine man is very free,” he said—just as the wild-haired designer burst outside for a smoke, laughing and relieved.

Wearing a standard-issue, backstage-friendly black crewneck sweater, Rider wasn’t exactly channeling the improvisational look of the brand he’s re-engineered in only a handful of shows. He assumed the role of artistic director in 2025, succeeding Slimane. Before taking Celine’s reins, he put in time under Nicolas Ghesquière at Balenciaga (2004–08) and at Phoebe Philo–era Celine (2008–17). But the secret to the Rider Effect—his unique ability to conjure clarity from chaos—was a lesson he picked up during his tenure at Ralph Lauren.

Rider worked for the all-American designer as creative director of women’s Polo Ralph Lauren from 2018 until he decamped for Celine. Early on, he threw himself into staging his first “rig room.” A very Ralph tradition, the rig room is an installation of a fashion collection designed to be presented to Lauren internally—a fully immersive world complete with music, decor, props, and reference photos. Rider worked on his first one incessantly for two months. When Lauren arrived, he looked around in silence while Rider stood beside him, sweating in a navy blazer.

At last, Lauren asked, “Why do you want to confuse people?”

“I think about that a lot,” confesses Rider when we speak in a circular antechamber at Celine’s Paris headquarters a few days after the show. Disappointing Lauren was a turning point for Rider. He had gotten the job designing Polo after 14 years in the upper echelons of European fashion. “Mixing references and confusing people was part of the game,” he remembers. “You elevated yourself and your brand through adjacencies and pastiche. Ralph was the total opposite.”

“I definitely appreciated going back to the States and hearing from a master: Be clear,” says Rider. The ongoing tension of his current work lies in resolving his tendency toward anarchy with a desire for legibility. His Celine is layered and unfettered and fun. But it is also as clear, as the French say, as water on rocks.

Sitting in the same room where he and Philo “dumped our bags and met people” during his first stint at Celine, Rider looks calm and perfectly at home. Now that he’s at the helm of the 81-year-old LVMH maison founded by Céline and Richard Vipiana, the “rotonde” room has a few framed New Yorker cartoons propped on a wicker bench, some personalized thank-you cards to send, a pack of cigs, Evian, and not much else. Twinkly and alert, with no phone in sight, Rider wears a blue button-up, dark khaki pants, black canvas trainers, a gold Cartier watch, and some chunky rings. His hair sticks straight up like one of his inspirations: Isaac Mizrahi.

Mizrahi’s Unzipped documentary, which recently celebrated its 30th anniversary, was one of the references for the summer show. So, too, was another canonic ’90s documentary, Paris Is Burning, about the queer ballroom scene in late-’80s Manhattan. Both films look at the human side of fabulosity, something that interests Rider. Brands are the creations of curious, restless minds, and the best transcend desire, attracting something close to faith. Rider himself has been one of those believers, lusting after Ghesquière’s Balenciaga during his first real job, when he was just an underpaid teacher. (“I would have killed for something from there,” he says.) In his show notes, he wrote about “our desires and frustrations. Memories, moments that made us love fashion. Moments where you get a glimpse of possibility.”

In practice, that looks like something you want to buy, but that has soul. Rider, like Lauren and Mizrahi, is a designer who makes clothing and accessories that feel just familiar enough to strike a nostalgic chord, but fresh enough that they can’t be replaced by trawling The RealReal. In his first Celine collection, shown in July 2025 under a sudden Parisian downpour, the looks bore a healthy pinch of Polo-honed prep: red blazers, diagonal-stripe ties, pressed jeans, loafers. Now that style is officially everywhere, with every middle-class menswear brand and fast-fashion factory churning out their own versions.

What separates Rider’s Celine is that it gets men excited to dress, says Nordstrom men’s fashion director Jian DeLeon: “It triggers that lizard-brain impulse that inspires them to shop. They didn’t realize they wanted a bright-blue military jacket, and then when they see it in store, Rider’s design nuances—like oversized, ruched sleeves and slightly different blocks of color in the fabric—further satisfy the kinds of bells and whistles that men’s fashion enthusiasts nerd out about.”

In his first solo men’s presentation this past January, Rider brought his Ralph-perfected merchandising flair to Celine for a rig-room-esque installation of styling combinations that shouldn’t have worked—like a paisley tie layered beneath a red-string, hippie pendant necklace—and yet, did. Loafers in every shade played to an audience of ’90s kids who lusted after stacks of Benetton sweaters. Army jackets became accessories, belted around waists. It was American mall culture whipped through a blender with ready-to-wear refinement.

Rider’s Celine made an impact even earlier with his very first outing, the co-ed spring 2026 collection, shown in mid-2025. Soon after that range was available, Paul Anthony Kelly, who played nouveau John F. Kennedy Jr. in Ryan Murphy’s hit FX series Love Story, wore a Kennedy-ish Celine look: a white Oxford shirt, red-and-navy striped tie, navy blazer, jeans, white socks, loafers. The message was clear: Kelly had arrived—and so had Rider. Kelly’s stylist, Warren Alfie Baker, says he got hundreds of messages from people saying, “Oh my God, I need to go and buy that.” Why did he think it hit so hard? “What Michael does really well is it feels relatable,” Baker explained. “Everybody wanted to replicate it or have a version of it.”

Baker, who styles classic leading-men types like Glen Powell, Andrew Scott, and Andrew Garfield, says Rider’s work was heating up in Hollywood ahead of the fall awards season. “When you see a runway with 45 looks, and you’re like, ‘I could actually use 40 of them,’ that’s the dream scenario.”

Slimane had introduced menswear to Celine in 2018 for the first time in the brand’s history with skinny black jeans, skinnier black ties, and shrunken leather jackets—an aesthetic driven more by rock-and-roll than red carpets. When he brought the brand to Los Angeles in late 2022 for an 87-look fashion show-cum-concert at the Wiltern, rockers including Iggy Pop, the Strokes, Interpol, and the Kills wore Slimane’s indie-sleaze uniforms to perform. “Celine’s past has been very skinny. Maybe some guys wouldn’t have known that they could wear it,” conceded Baker.

Rider’s Celine offers more elbow room, literally and otherwise. “It’s not such a rigid idea of how a man should dress,” says fashion commentator and stylist Nicky Bell, who has styled Mark Ronson in several Rider looks, including a custom leather jacket for this year’s Brit Awards. “Other menswear brands are too rigid: They want you to be this really formal, masculine man, or they want you to be super androgynous. He lands in this in-between space.”

Born in 1980 to two do-gooder attorney parents in Washington DC, Rider was raised in an intellectual, progressive household well outside the fashion bubble. Musing on why he’s still drawn to things that are a little off, and the stalls at the flea market with “the mangiest, strangest assortment of clothing,” he says. “My parents are not materialistic in any way. There are nice things around, and they make things. My mom’s an incredible cook, there’s needlepoint, my dad [told] great stories. But it wasn’t a situation where aesthetic perfection was the goal.”

“I was always in my own strange lane,” says Rider. “Everybody who seemed cool to me was on their own path.” His older cousin introduced him to the Grateful Dead, a lifelong love. Rider was, naturally, first drawn to the T-shirts—“the merch always brings me in”—but then became fascinated by the totality of Deadhead culture. “I was very attracted to the experimentation and freedom and fewer rules,” he says. “I like color, I like people who customize things, and I like weirdos.”

The Dead were a gateway into an adolescence full of experimentation. “I had all the phases,” Rider says, from Birkenstocks worn with Thorlo hiking socks, to hip-hop streetwear, to skate style that he finessed in shops like Green Barrel in Georgetown and Stüssy in the suburb of Potomac. He also dabbled in the all-American look he’d later help shape at Polo. “We went to public school and were proud of it, so preppy was a bad word, but everybody at my school worshipped Polo. They just wore it differently, and we mixed it all.”

Rider’s still mixing. “It’s always been a lot of fun for me to get dressed,” he says. When he lived in New York City while at Ralph Lauren, he had standing movie nights at the Battery Park City cinema with the photographer Tommy Ton and designer Trevor Ballin (who works with him now at Celine), both friends. Ton, a street-style savant, loved seeing the outfits Rider would pull off at the cinema, like ankle-chopped Uggs with an Hermès shawl, or Grateful Dead bear–embroidered shorts. Levy says he could see Rider’s own vacation wardrobe in the women’s looks of the summer collection. “He shows up to dinner in caftans and sandals, or harem pants.”

Which can be hard to square with the fact that Rider went to Brown University with the intention of becoming a teacher. He moved to Oakland after graduating and taught ninth grade at a charter school. “Everyone was bigger than me,” says the petite designer. Living in the Bay Area, going out a lot, and experimenting with clothing, he eventually felt a pull to the creative world that he couldn’t shake, which would lead to him interning with his then hero, Ghesquière.

Rider, the former teacher, remains a perpetual student. He tells me, with a glance at his PR minder, that the kind of fashion profiles he loves—like Judith Thurman’s unvarnished 2005 New Yorker story on Rei Kawakubo—aren’t really possible anymore. In the post-Galliano-meltdown, recession-hardened luxury landscape, publicly traded conglomerates protect their creative directors from criticism like the precious assets that they are.

So he painstakingly protects his distance—but doesn’t sacrifice his sense of humor in the process. You’ll see it in the pop of outrageous purple, a woolly outdoorsy fleece, those shimmering suits. There’s a sense that being too serious is just kind of sad. He likes when people talk about Celine as “good-time clothes” that they wear when they go out. “I would be mortified if anyone thought silliness was on the menu,” Rider says. Still, “Things are very funny to us, and that has to be felt somehow. I think humor is really stylish.”

Eons have passed, seemingly, since Rider interned in the menswear department of Balenciaga in the mid-aughts. “Fashion for men was very fringe then,” he says, remembering that the men’s collection at the label totaled maybe a dozen looks. At the time, Slimane’s strict silhouettes for Dior Homme were in; Rider wore some of that, along with the stiff selvedge APC jeans that became part of the ascent of #menswear. He recalls Ghesquière being obsessed at the time with making the ideal men’s wardrobe, from button-ups to parkas.

“Menswear has completely opened up now,” Rider says. “It’s a different ball game. Because it’s so much broader now, and people have phones; people everywhere have access to so much and are engaged in more conversations. Not always for good, but it moves. The rules can move, and the goalposts can move.”

Rider, after an almost Forrest Gump-y run of consistently being at the center of gravity—at Balenciaga, with Philo, and at Ralph Lauren—without having tried so hard to be there, is now the one doing the goalpost-moving. And he has no interest in hard rules or self-inflicted limitations.

“I think a lot of people who do this thing end up living, or trying to live out, the same story over and over,” he says.

He resists sheeplike notions of what’s considered cool—“this artist, this pottery, this lamp, this show space collaboration,” as he puts it. And he’s careful not to follow the flock too closely. “Paris is amazing, but Paris is insular,” says Rider. “Everyone’s eating at the same canteen, gossiping about the same thing. There’s a gigantic world out there.”

So Rider keeps doing his own thing. He revels in American pop culture—he’s just as passionate about going to the multiplex near his weekend home in Normandy to see the latest Wicked as he is paging through those old World of Interiors magazines. He’s started weight-lifting, in the evenings. Learning Arabic is on his bucket list. And often he finds himself going back to his roots for inspiration.

Every summer, he returns to Martha’s Vineyard, where his family has had a house since the 1970s. He loves its isolation, and its realness: “Against all odds, it has remained what it is. There’s no bridge, the airport’s still tiny, 85 percent of it is protected. There’s no Balenciaga.” On Martha’s Vineyard, he likes being out on the water.

“The most American thing about me is that I like to paddle,” he says, laughing. “I’m my best self in a canoe.” ✦

A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “This Quiet American Has Fashion’s Attention.”

#6560. Your Exclusive First Look at the Official 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie' Hall Merch

“I will keep rolling down until my best shirt rolls off,” warbles Cameron Winter on “The Rolling Stone,” the opening track of his 2024 solo debut Heavy Metal. That album later became the basis of the Geese frontman’s historic December 2025 performance at Carnegie Hall, which was filmed and subsequently turned into a captivating concert film by Oscar-winning director Paul Thomas Anderson. A year later, Winter—and perhaps you—will now have a new best shirt to roll off.

PTA’s Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which was shot on 35mm and 16mm film, will hit select theaters nationwide on Friday. As a reward to the Geeseheads and steadfast cinephiles who attend the 35mm screenings, distributor Janus Films produced a limited-edition run of merch (many such cases!) that can only be purchased IRL at select participating theaters. Which is to say, acquiring this merch…takes miles.

But if you’re looking at the Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall T-shirts ($40) and baseball hats ($35) and thinking, “Wow, those look a lot like the maximalist, erudite wares from Boot Boyz Biz,” that’s because they were in fact designed by two of the Chicago brand’s current outposts, Now-Time and Mike’s Deli.

In an email, the Now-Time/Mike’s Deli team said that they drew inspiration from Carnegie Hall’s history and architecture. “We looked to the building itself as a visual archive to draw from, seeking forms that resonated with the performance across time,” they wrote. “Familiar architectural details took on a new heightened significance, knowing what was happening inside. In Carnegie Hall’s classic horseshoe layout we saw the camera’s panoramic intent. Outside on the 19th-century facade we found typographic elements that paralleled the energy of the event.” A very Winteresque explanation, in a way. Ideal for any enigmatic T-shirt enthusiast.

If you, too, would like to participate in the seeking forms and panoramic intent of Winter’s moving piano stylings on one winter’s night in Manhattan, you better start a-walking to the nearest 35mm-equipped cinema near you.

GQ staffers Jordan Bowman and Gerald Ortiz testing out the merchandise.

#6559. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6558. What You Need to Know About Japanese Knives

The popularity of Japanese knives in home and commercial kitchens has exploded in the last few years, and for good reason: A lot of them outperform their Western counterparts in kitchen tests. Western-style knives are bulkier, all-purpose kitchen tools—years ago, it would be common for many chefs to use the heavy bolster near the heel of the blade to crack open a can of tomatoes during service. Japanese knives (and Japanese-style knives produced by manufacturers elsewhere) are designed with precision cuts in mind and usually have a specific purpose. However, because they’re designed with that specificity in mind, it can be tricky to know what you need and what you’ll use.

Thankfully, we’ve reviewed a wide variety of Japanese-style knives for Bon Appétit and have assembled a roundup to help you identify exactly what your kitchen needs. While there are more styles of Japanese knives than those listed here, these options have all been thoroughly tested, giving us the confidence to speak to each knife’s utility. Before we jump into specific styles, however, it’s useful to give a quick rundown on some of the broad strokes of what makes a Japanese-style knife unique.

Many Japanese knives are designed for push cuts or pull-through slicing rather than the rocking chop of a heavy Western chef’s knife. They tend to have a straighter edge than their Western counterparts, making them slightly less adept at speeding through a mince of herbs, but more precise in their cuts. Most Japanese-style knives also feature a sheep’s-foot tip that curves down to the point, giving the user more control over fine-point work.

Japanese knives are often made with a harder steel than their Western counterparts. Harder steel helps a knife’s edge retain sharpness, which lets manufacturers use steeper sharpening angles for a finer edge. This helps most Japanese knives slice more delicately than Western knives, though harder steel can chip on material like ice or bone.

Traditional Japanese-style knives are only sharpened on one side, giving them a much finer edge than the 50/50 bevel of Western-style knives that are sharpened on both sides. Some modern Japanese knife makers have pivoted to a 50/50 style bevel for ease of sharpening; however, when you’re shopping, you’ll encounter plenty of knives with 70/30 bevel with the inside edge (the left edge for a right-handed knife) sharpened at a steeper angle. A 70/30 bevel is easier to maintain than a single-bevel but offers a sharper edge than a 50/50 bevel.

Many traditional Japanese kitchen knives feature a wa-style handle—an octagonal wood handle that envelops a hidden knife tang (the metal part of the knife that connects to the handle). Wa-style handles help keep knives lighter and nimbler, while many Western-style knives use full-tang construction, adding weight and heft to the blade. Many modern Japanese knife makers, though, combine full-tang knife handles with Japanese blade shapes to create a hybrid-style knife that’s both durable and adept at slicing.

The gyuto, or Japanese chef’s knife, originated in Japan in the early 1900s, when French cooking began to gain popularity in a rapidly modernizing country. This knife style took cues from the traditional French chef’s knife and combined them with elements of traditional Japanese knife making. The resulting Japanese take on a chef’s knife was primarily designed for slicing meat, though it also features a curved edge that makes it easy to chop herbs. Compared to a Western chef’s knife, the gyuto has a straighter blade and a drop point tip with a lower overall profile. This is primarily designed so that the user can place the knife’s tip on the cutting board and draw it through food, taking advantage of the gyuto’s sharp edge and thin blade for precision slicing. But while the gyuto excels at slicing meat, its general shape makes it an overall great pick to anchor your knife collection, and many home cooks opt for a gyuto as their daily driver over a traditional chef’s knife.

We’ve long been fans of the gyuto fan here at Bon Appétit, with MAC’s Professional Hollow Ground Chef’s Knife topping our chef’s knife review for years. For a wicked sharp, more traditional option, we really like the Kazan Arare by Shibata gyuto, which impressed us so much we had to give it its own review.

Increasingly common as a part of brands’ knife sets, the santoku knife is a relatively modern knife shape, first appearing in the 1940s or so. Nicknamed the three virtues knife, the santoku draws on the gyuto, nakiri, and deba to create a well-rounded utility knife that’s great for cutting meat, fish, and vegetables. Typically, these knives feature a pretty steep sheep’s-foot tip for precision point work, a tall heel for push cuts, and just enough curve for pull-through slicing and rock-chopping. A santoku knife is great for well-rounded utility work—think cutting cheese and an apple for a snack, slicing leftover roasted chicken to make a sandwich, or dicing an onion for a curry.

Typically, we like a santoku knife that’s between six and seven inches, so it contrasts with the longer gyuto. Our favorite overall model is the MAC Professional Santoku Knife, but if you’d like a razor-sharp version with a traditional wa-style handle, we love the Kazan Ginsan Nashiji Santoku.

Nakiri knives have a straight edge and a sturdy spine, specifically designed for chopping vegetables. Sometimes referred to as a vegetable cleaver, the nakiri excels at push cuts, making it great for both matchsticking carrots and breaking down tough-skinned squash. Since most gyutos feature thin blades and fine edges, the nakiri also holds a spot in the Japanese knife lineup as a tougher, heavier knife for more demanding tasks. Traditional nakiri knives may also feature a blunt, rounded tip, which can be rotated against the cutting board to create a smooth, chopping motion.

The Tojiro DP Damascus Nakiri is by far our overall favorite tested nakiri knife for its extremely sharp edge and overall balance, but it’s also pricey. We also really like the Tojiro Classic nakiri, though it can have stock issues due to its popularity and price point.

The deba knife is a traditional Japanese knife designed for fish butchery. Unlike a Western fillet knife, which is designed to be flexible and nimble, the deba is a heavy, sturdy blade with a thick spine that gives the heel of the blade a cleaver-like feel. But a deba knife is also designed for precision slicing, and it usually features a traditional single-bevel edge. That single-bevel edge allows the knife to come to a finer point than a double-bevel edge, and the sheep’s-foot tip adds to the deba knife’s ability to portion out delicate fish fillets as well.

We haven’t tested deba knives because they require a bit of knowledge and skill to use them for breaking down whole fish, but if you’re intrigued by the shape and want a cleaver-like knife for your kitchen, the Seki Mago Roku Deba from Kai is an affordable, solid option. Otherwise, we think most people would be better served looking to a nakiri or santoku knife.

Named for the French word petite, which means small, the petty knife is often a replica of the gyuto, just in a much, much smaller form. Most petty knives are around five inches long and feature a thin, lightly curved blade with a drop point tip and heel just tall enough to keep your fingers from bashing into the cutting board. Petty knives are great utility knives for small tasks, like dicing a shallot, slicing garlic, or slicing herbs, but they’re also long and nimble enough to be great slicers. Unless you do a lot of handheld turning and peeling, a petty knife is a great replacement for a paring knife in your lineup.

We found that both the MAC Professional Petty Knife and the Tojiro Classic Petty Knife were sharp enough to slice a steak while still being the perfect size to slice strawberries for your morning yogurt bowl.

Traditionally a fisherman’s knife used for all sorts of purposes on the boat, the funayuki is an old-school knife shape that predates the gyuto and santoku, and it likely helped inspire both shapes. The traditional funayuki is a shorter knife, around seven inches long, with a narrow, pointed tip and a tall heel. They are santoku-sized but gyuto-shaped. Unlike the deba knife, which was a heavy, single-bevel knife used for fish butchery, the funayuki was designed to be light and nimble so that fishermen could fillet their lunch while at sea. These days, most home cooks might pick up a funayuki as a secondary, shorter gyuto, or opt for this shape over a santoku as an all-purpose utility knife with a narrower tip.

Though it’s not as common in modern kitchens, one of our favorite Japanese chef’s knives is the Akiru-Saku Funayuki Gyuto, which is more traditionally shaped like a funayuki but is advertised as a gyuto since the two shapes are so similar.

The kiritsuke is a Japanese slicing knife with an angular “sword tip” that allows the user to make precision cuts. The initial design combined a long slicing shape and tall heel, making the kiritsuke a hybrid knife, similar to the santoku. For most people, the kiritsuke will be a version of an all-purpose chef’s knife that could take the place of a gyuto as a daily driver, with the big difference coming in the shape of the tip.

When reviewing chef’s knives, we found that the Shun Classic Kiritsuke was a great all-purpose chef’s knife with a unique tip that some people might prefer over a gyuto, since it curves upward more like a Western chef’s knife and allows for more of a rock chop motion.

Boning and fillet knives are often unitaskers that don’t see much use unless you’re a fan of home butchery, but the Japanese honesuki is an even more specialized boning knife shape. Designed specifically for poultry, the honesuki is a steep, wedge-shaped knife with a very fine point and a tall heel. The goal is to have a knife that’s delicate enough to slip between a chicken joint while being sturdy enough to cut through cartilage. While the honesuki was designed for a specific purpose, we find that this shape is more versatile and can be swapped in for a petty knife for other small chopping and dicing tasks in ways that a curved fillet knife can’t.

We like the MAC Professional Honesuki as a great option that could tackle most boning-knife tasks while remaining sharp and versatile enough for utility work. If you find yourself breaking down a whole chicken while also wanting a strawberry-slicing knife, the honesuki could be a nonconventional multitasker.

#6557. Chanel’s Watches & Fine Jewelry Dinner Christened Daniel Humm’s New Hotspot

“Yes, it’s my first time here, too,” was the refrain repeatedly heard around the room at Humm on Hudson Street on Tuesday evening, as guests stole glances at their Première Galon watches to count down the minutes to dinner. After a candlelit cocktail hour, right on cue, at 8 p.m., the moment had come to experience Daniel Humm’s new restaurant, some two years in the making.

Chanel has been keeping New York’s best-dressed guests busy as of late: The last few weeks alone have seen outings for the Museum of Modern Art’s Film Benefit, the Dia Art Foundation, the Women’s Prize Trust, and Tribeca Through Her Lens. This time around, the annual Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner was as good an excuse as any for the group to get dolled up and enjoy a pause before the busiest season of all.

Sarah Pidgeon, who became an official ambassador for the house’s watches and fine jewelry last year, was among the earliest to arrive. For the occasion, the Love Story star donned a Coco Crush necklace and bracelets. The night was also a chance for the actress to reunite with fellow Ryan Murphy-universe newcomer Ella Beatty, fresh off her acclaimed turn as the notorious Lizzie Borden.

Though the restaurant has been open for just a month and change—Chanel’s get-together being the first brand event hosted there—word has traveled fast about its menu. Luckily, the evening’s sampling incorporated the soon-to-be-renowned caviar-topped miniature bagels, which, along with the disco-tiled bathroom, seem destined for Instagram Stories fame.

A crowd, including Ella Rubin, Jack Harlow, and Quen Blackwell, settled in, drinking up the oxblood and velvet interiors, co-designed by Pierre Yovanovitch and Humm’s longtime friend, Italian artist Francesco Clemente. Clemente—yes, the namesake of the bar at Humm’s Eleven Madison Park—covered the ceilings in hand-painted stars, bricks, tiles, and trains. Works by Louise Bourgeois, Rashid Johnson, and Roni Horn round out the feast for the eyes.

As chocolate mousses and endless trays of espresso martinis did the rounds and the clock struck 10 p.m., Pidgeon stood to introduce a surprise performance by breakthrough Canadian singer girlsweetvoiced to end the night. “I was listening to her earlier today while walking around New York, and she captures something that’s very tender and honest in her stories,” Pidgeon said. “Her music is both singular and expansive and entirely her own.”

After girlsweetvoiced serenaded the room with three songs—“Cranberry,” “Spearmint,” and “Tonight,” her Joni Mitchell–approved single that samples “California”—the night drew to a close. Guests slowly made their way toward the exit, taking engraved gold matchboxes home with them as a keepsake of a reliably good time with Chanel, no matter the theme.

#6556. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6555. At the Races: It's almost over

By Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Voters are weighing in on whether to keep Republicans in control of Congress or give some power to Democrats amid mounting signs of dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump.

Democrats, who have expanded both the House and Senate battleground maps, are optimistic about their chances, while Republicans are hoping their base voters turn out — and help them defy the polls once again.

The expanded battleground map was evident in our final rankings of the most vulnerable senators, which included Sens. Roger Marshall of Kansas, Darline Graham of South Carolina and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, three states that weren’t exactly expected to be part of the battleground at the beginning of the year.

Some of House Republicans’ best pickup opportunities come in districts that were redrawn in their favor, which is reflected in our final list of the most vulnerable House incumbents. Just two Democrats— Florida’s Darren Soto and Alabama’s Shomari Figures — rank among the 10 most endangered House members, while Republicans from the nation’s most competitive swing seats occupy most of the other spots.

Speaker Mike Johnson has spent the past several weeks crisscrossing the country hoping to save his narrow majority. He appeared Monday night with Rep. Jen Kiggans in the same Virginia district where Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat, campaigned on Saturday. Earlier in the day, Johnson returned to Eastern North Carolina, home to a costly rematch between Democratic Rep. Don Davis and Republican Laurie Buckhout. Johnson also held a rally in a neighboring district that Trump would have carried by 14 points, a sign of GOP vulnerabilities even in conservative terrain. The speaker will begin Election Day in South Texas, where Republicans are hoping to flip two House seats while preserving another.

To mark Election Day, we’ve taken a look back over the past two years and identified 15 key moments that shaped the midterm campaign. We also have five questions we hope the election results will help us answer, including whether redistricting pays off for Republicans and how key constituencies that supported Trump and Republicans two years ago vote this time. And Roll Call photojournalists Bill Clark and Tom Williams shared the most memorable and striking images from their time on the trail this cycle.

Of course, it hasn’t been a quiet end to the campaign. Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, who unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for Senate this year, sent shockwaves across both parties Sunday when she appeared with and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over primary rival Abdul El-Sayed.

That followed a major development in the Alaska Senate race, after The New York Times reported that aides to Democrat Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate who shares a name with Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. A federal judge on Sunday rejected a lawsuit from the Trump administration, which sought to delay certification of the Senate election if the incumbent Sullivan loses, as our colleague Michael Macagnone reported.

If your preferred way to watch results roll in is with a crowd, CQ Roll Call’s Nina Heller has a rundown of D.C. bars that will be airing election night results, many of which are offering deals on drinks and food.

Stay tuned to the Roll Call website for results and immediate takeaways. At the Races will be back in your inbox as usual on Thursday as we break the results down and look ahead to the next Congress.

After all, 2028 is right around the corner.

#6554. Willy Chavarria Debuts His Dream “Bitchy Little Bags”

Are you a woman chasing the Willy Chavarria look? You’ll want to channel a Hitchcock heroine—Tippi Hedren is his favorite. Elongating skirt? Check. Strong-shouldered blouse or jacket? Done. Swooping french twist? Looking up Youtube tutorials now. But what about the classic handbag hitched up in the crook of your arm? Now, that can be yours, too.

Launched this morning on willychavarria.com, two new styles—the Bronca and the W Slouch—mark the New York designer’s official debut in the handbag space. Despite the pretty regular appearance of bags at his runway shows (both the Bronca and the W Slouch were seen at his spring 2027 menswear outing), introducing the category was a long time coming for Chavarria. “I’ve just been really timid about launching bags because it’s such a big thing,” he tells Vogue. “I never wanted to have a bag that ends up at the back of the store, doesn’t get the attention it needs—we just kind of pulled back and we said, okay, we’re going to launch this very soft bag that feels good.” Hence, only two styles, and direct-to-consumer only.

The Bronca is “sassy,” “a bitchy little bag,” even, and that’s just how Chavarria likes it. Available in pink, blue, black, and chocolate brown, it features a rolled leather handle with a set of keys dangling from the clasp. His dream girl to sport it is his forever muse Bianca Jagger; he’s fantasized about her pairing it with the iconic Yves Saint Laurent white wedding suit she wore to marry Mick in 1971.

In contrast, Chavarria says the W Slouch, available in green, chocolate brown, and black, is geared more towards his menswear customers. It comes with a detachable padded long strap, making it ideal for trekking across town with half of your belongings. To style it, he suggests following the wrong shoe theory. “I think it’s really cool with a tough look for a guy to have a bag that throws it off,” he says. “I always love those looks that just make you do a double take.”

Prior to today’s release, the designer has produced a W-embossed leather tote, some clutches, and a few coin purses, but he doesn’t look at those offerings in the same light. “This is more of me looking at [the category] as a business opportunity and building a plan and thinking about how I can grow this business,” he says.

It helps that with every collection, he’s dabbling in womenswear more and more. For his women customers, he sees a handbag as the perfect way in. “The brand is still small enough that I’m very careful about adding new categories, but as I’ve seen my womenswear business grow, it makes sense from a strategic standpoint to add a bag to the collection that actually enhances the full collection. And maybe she just buys the bag, maybe that’s all she wants.”

Though Chavarria is personally partial to a razor-sharp evening clutch, he doesn’t have plans to expand into additional silhouettes anytime soon. “I want to sit with these for a while,” he says. “I want to get these in the market and have people wearing them and get comfortable with them, and then maybe add on some little offspring, some little babies that go inside.” A nesting doll of handbag options await.

#6553. What a 43-Year-Old Server and Drag Queen Eats on $63K CAD in Toronto, Ontario

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one anonymous reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today's Receipt, we follow a 43-year-old server and drag queen in Toronto, Ontario. Keep reading for his receipts.

The financesThe dietThe expensesThe diary

What is your occupation? Server, Drag Queen

What city and state do you live in? Toronto, ON

What is your annual salary, if you have one? Girl, I have no idea. Waiting tables brings in around $60K CAN, and performing in bars, nightclubs and drag brunches probably makes me another $3K, but all those sweat-and-glitter-covered bills get stuffed under a mattress, so who knows?

How much is one paycheck, after taxes? Let’s call it an even thousand dollars.

How often are you paid? (e.g., weekly) Weekly or biweekly

What are your approximate fixed monthly expenses beyond food? (i.e., rent, subscriptions, bills)

Do you follow a certain diet or have dietary restrictions? I avoid salt and gluten as much as possible

What are the grocery staples you always buy, if any? Eggs, gluten-free pasta, bananas, bone broth, greens, yogurt. I almost always have boiled eggs ready in the fridge, a tub of yogurt, some dark berries, and bananas to keep me fueled up. If I’m going to cook, it’s pasta or meat and veggies.

How often in a week do you dine out versus cook at home? I work in an upscale Italian restaurant and the food is exceptional. I eat there three or four times a week and have the cholesterol levels to prove it. At 50% off any menu items (minus the $128 porterhouse steak) it’s a bargain to eat delicious, mostly healthy cooked meals. I love going out socially or alone and do so almost weekly.

How often in a week did you dine out while growing up? Once a month? Rural Alberta didn’t have a ton of dining-out choices

How often in a week did your parents or guardians cook at home? Daily. My mom’s (and occasionally my dad’s) cooking was excellent. Nothing fancy, but a real meat-and-potatoes type menu that kept us going

10 a.m. My annual sinus infection came early, and I’ve been sick since Saturday. I’m trying to break my morning caffeine habit, but today I’m too lazy and run down. I hydrate with lemon water while sipping an Americano with brown sugar. Between the coffee and the illness I don’t have much of an appetite. I forage on peanut butter and pumpkin seeds while shuffling around my apartment.

4 p.m. A thought occurs to me: Let’s heal this body with some miso and wasabi. I order sushi from Kibo down the street. It’s takeout, so I am forced to don clothing and walk down the street. I pick up 2-for-1 dynamite rolls, chicken gyoza dumplings, miso soup, the obligatory green salad that comes with it all. and a spicy salmon combo. $44

As I’m feeling sorry for myself on my walk back home, I stop at the corner store for a bottle of Blake Boulevard Sauvignon Blanc. $21

10 a.m. I know that I have a shift at the restaurant today, so I’m holding my head up and pretending that I'm not at death's door. A banana-and-blueberry yogurt provide the gas I need to leave the house to get provisions.

We’re out of coffee beans! I have two espresso machines because I am a complete coffee snob. Machine number one, my favorite, is a De’Longhi manual espresso maker, a tall, silver tower with a handle on the side. I grind my own beans for this. Machine number two is a Nespresso Virtuo. It requires aluminum pods stuffed with coffee. It’s sleek and makes a lovely crema, but it’s never hot enough for me. The pods vary between $1.12 and $1.50 each.

On the way home I stop in at St. Clair Avenue Fruit Market for some of my usuals: bok choy, celery, dates, rapini, bananas, and a container of feta, for fun. $31.75

3 p.m. Before work I load up on cold meds even though they make me feel like a bobblehead. Somewhere between 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. I ask my chef to sneak me some arancini to avoid passing out while bringing some nice folks their wine and dinner. Our arancini are filled with mozzarella, rolled in a saffron risotto, and plated with tomato sauce. Retail $24, but for me it’s $12.

10 a.m. Americano, brown sugar, lemon water. I have a friend coming in from out of town and she is fully aware how ill I am, and I feel as though she may need a snack after her two-plus-hour drive, so I pop down to another cute hot spot on my street, Le Bleu. I may or may not also have a huge crush on the owner, Iman. I pick up vegan baklava, vegan banana bread, a caprese sandwich for her and prosciutto for me. I try to make small talk with Iman while he packs up my order, but he’s so handsome I end up muttering and mumbling my thank-yous while I stumble out the door. $25.76

6 p.m. Reservations for two at a vegetarian restaurant, Planta Yorkville. I am not a vegetarian. I had mid to low expectations. Guys, this place was incredible.

Delicious regular and zero-proof cocktails. A Cosmic Colada for me: coconut water, lemon, blueberry, and pineapple. For my friend: the Tokyo Blossom made with sake, gin, lychee liquor, and grapefruit tonic.

The unagi eggplant was so good I almost ordered a second one; we also ordered spicy tuna roll (some kind of juiced-up watermelon substitution), miso soup, and bang-bang broccoli. I ordered a chocolate brownie and a sticky toffee pudding for dessert—the latter was so big it was almost comical. They also stuffed an entire ice cream cone full of vanilla ice cream upside down onto my pudding. I finished about a quarter of it.

After she leaves and the day progresses I realize I am in no shape to work. Thankfully someone takes my serving shift so I don’t have to go and cough all over our lovely patrons.

6 p.m. My appetite has been suffering, but eventually I whip up one of my favorites: a bean medley, chickpeas, celery, olive oil, and feta salad.

8 p.m. As the sun sets and the self pity sinks in deeper, I throw a trench coat over my pajamas and scurry down to the store to get another favorite, a bottle of Te Henga Sauvignon Blanc. $19.45

10 a.m. Another Americano and lemon water.

1 p.m. At this point in the week, I am so sick of tea I never want to see it again. I’ve been trying to stave off whatever I have with honey/lemon/ginger tea, and I’m over it. That was lunch, I guess.

8 p.m. Guilty pleasure time! I call in an order for Little Caesars Chicago Deep Dish Meat Treat pizza, an order of hot wings, and a ginger ale. Pure class and total nutrition. The good news is that while attempting to remain unseen, I happen to run into someone I’ve been chatting with on a dating app. Oh, did I say good? I meant horrific. $39.77

10 a.m. Americano. Lemon Water. I’m a creature of habit, okay?

12 p.m. Bananas, blueberries, leftover bean salad, ginger tea.

3 p.m. I’m at work early, because we have new menu items. At pre-shift, the chef makes one of each and we discuss and sample it. A prime rib–chuck burger with scamorza and tomato bomba, lamb pizza with basil pesto, steak tartare, Atlantic cod and potato risotto, and mushroom-and-pea-stuffed ravioli. Some call this “product knowledge.” I call it a free meal(s).

8:45 p.m. Despite all my newfound product knowledge, I still get hungry halfway through my shift. Chef makes me a bulgur, kale, and roasted beet salad with a 7-oz. flatiron steak. $22

10:45 p.m. Shift done, head feeling like a block of ice, I sneak off to the market before heading home to grab a bottle of Squealing Pig Sauvignon Blanc. $22

10 a.m. Pretty much right after I open my eyes, I get a lovely text from a friend; “Wanna get breakfast?” She knows I’ve been sick and we haven’t caught up in a while. She is informed that I will be wearing my now-uniform of pajamas and trench coat.

11 a.m. Three eggs, toast, and bacon from a pub by my house. No culinary awards will be given out here, but it did what it was supposed to do. The bill for both meals with coffee and a couple of spicy Bloody Caesars came to $50.

7 p.m. Another go-to when I’m feeling down or simply have the craving is to simmer some rice noodles in a broth and add miso paste. I stir in fresh chopped bok choy, green onions, and a couple of cut-up hard-boiled eggs. I think I’m gonna make it.

#6552. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6550. 5 Cozy Meals Our Editors Make With Boxed Stuffing

Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month, it’s all about boxed stuffing.

Few Thanksgiving dishes inspire as many strong opinions as stuffing-slash-dressing. In a baking dish or the bird itself? Sourdough or white bread? Fresh herbs or dried? Sausage or nah? There are the purists, who insist on drying their own bread, chopping aromatics, and seasoning everything from scratch. Then there are the Stove Top loyalists, who grew up on that unmistakable red box and remain fiercely faithful. Site director Rachel Tepper Paley is firmly in the latter camp. “My late father considered boxed Stove Top the Platonic ideal of stuffing, so I grew up with the uber-savory stuff on every Thanksgiving table,” she says. “We continue to serve it every year in his honor.”

And then there’s a particularly resourceful subset of boxed-stuffing devotees: the maximalists who see the box as a pantry staple, not just a holiday shortcut. Our editors happen to be among them. Read on for all the ways they’re thinking outside the box.

The first time I tried my colleague Jesse Szewczyk’s Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet in the Test Kitchen, I immediately started plotting all the occasions I could make it: Friendsgiving, a random Tuesday, football Sunday, date night. Its deliciousness caught me off guard. Jesse sears chicken thighs until golden and crisp, then uses the schmaltzy drippings (a.k.a. liquid gold) to season the boxed stuffing. Dotted with sweet-tart cranberry gems, then baked with the chicken nestled back in, it’s basically Thanksgiving in one pan—and a recipe I plan to make well beyond November. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

When I find myself with instant stuffing, I like to make a baked eggs situation. I’ll make the stuffing according to the box’s directions in a shallow oven-proof skillet. With the heat on (so the stuffing continues to crisp), I’ll toss in some greens like kale or spinach until they’re just barely wilted. Then I’ll use a spatula to make a couple divots throughout and crack an egg into each. From there, I’ll pop the skillet into a 375° oven and bake until the whites are set, about 15 minutes. A drizzle of green hot sauce and some salty feta crumble or sliced avocado, and I’m ready to eat. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

The way I see it, boxed stuffing mix is really close to a box of well-seasoned breadcrumbs. So why not use it as a savory panade that transforms lean ground turkey into tender meatballs? Senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk called this sheet-pan dinner Turkey and Stuffing Meatballs, but it honestly delivers all the flavors of Thanksgiving in one simple meal. You’ve got creamy baby Yukon gold potatoes and snappy green beans, plus a dipping sauce made from another autumn pantry staple, canned cranberry sauce, with lemon and honey to serve alongside. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

As a person who works in food media, I end up with my fair share of “what can I do with this?” ingredients. So while I firmly believe that no Thanksgiving dressing matters as much as my classic cornbread-and-biscuit version, I am no stranger to boxed stuffing. Frequently, it becomes a crust for baked fish. I’ve used Anna Stockwell’s easy no-recipe-required crispy fish method dozens of times since it first published, and it never disappoints. Best of all, you can use whatever bits and bobs you have lying around to build out the meal, and it’s relatively hands-off. Wins all around. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

For cozy season, there is nothing more comforting than carbs on carbs. I’ve always loved pasta with breadcrumbs (every which way), but leave it to senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk to make that classic combo even better: In this recipe, instead of using plain breadcrumbs or Italian seasoned ones, he swaps in stuffing mix blitzed in the food processor. Brilliant. It’s a highly flavorful topping for pasta with sausage and kale, a total delight for a cold night. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

#6548. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6545. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.
